utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning. The Registrar, could you please call the case for the ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-A, the Prosecutor versus Mladen Naletilic and Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Can everybody hear me, in particular, can the -- Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic follow the proceeding? I understand this is the case. So we can continue our hearing. When we did break yesterday, the Prosecutor had started its response to the submission of counsel for Martinovic. The Prosecution will have an hour today to continue and conclude its response. So I will give the floor to the Prosecution for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, my learned colleagues. I'll just set out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg wants to have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I take it you have concluded your remarks on the international armed conflict. Having done some research and having read carefully your remarks yesterday, in LiveNote it's page 124, it was at 5.35, that you stated that in Kordic and Cerkez in paragraph 311 implicitly Celebici and Tadic were overturned. Let me come back to this fundamental question of criminal law. I think it's absolutely undisputed that when it's a question of jurisdiction, then there is no question of mens rea at all, it's merely objective criteria. But isn't it true that I'm not speaking of the principle nullum crimen sine lege but I'm speaking about the principle of guilt, the fundamental principle of guilt, that when there is an element of crime that this element has in any event to be covered by the awareness of the perpetrator, or would you be able to give any example in criminal law where elements of crime are only seen as objective conditions for penalisation? I take it, to conclude the question, that in Kordic and Cerkez it was absolutely not necessary to discuss the factual question whether one of the accused, in this case, were aware that there was an armed conflict and in your discussion yesterday you also said that in your opinion, in the case before us, from the factual perspective it's no problem at all, but as you raised it as a legal fundamental question, I really want to know what is your -- exactly your proposition. Do you believe that a crime can be committed without the awareness of an element of crime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Schomburg. The question comes down to your -- for me the question comes down to: When you say an element of the crime, do you mean - or you're asking me - whether or not that element is a requisite element to be proved in relation to the accused or whether or not we can find things such as jurisdictional elements, chapeau elements or contextual elements that don't have to be proved in relation to the individual perpetrator. I tried to take a look at that issue in preparation for the hearing, and one matter which in my respectful submission remains unresolved is whether or not the perpetrator is required to know the widespread and systematic nature, for example, of the chapeau element or the contextual chapeau element, however you want to call it. It appears to be unclear only to the extent that in the Kunarac Appeals Chamber judgement the Court has held that what the perpetrator needs to know is that there was an attack against the civilian population and that his acts constitute part of the attack. Some Trial Chamber decisions including this one in Tuta, Stela, says he had to know the widespread and systematic nature of the attack. The Kunarac judgement doesn't specifically address that issue. It simply limits it to: He has to know of the attack and that he was part of it. That language, if I recall, was also duplicated in subsequent Appeals Chamber decisions that, to that extent, if the -- there is -- there is therefore a knowledge component, of course, but the knowledge component doesn't include, if that interpretation is correct, the widespread and systematic nature. In relation to -- I couldn't think of other contextual or jurisdictional elements, the nexus with the armed conflict, I think that's a jurisdictional element under our Statute. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this is absolutely undisputed and I think we shouldn't discuss it, but when we have, in fact, jurisdiction and we come to a concrete case, the question before us, why is it that in addition to other crimes under Article 5 or common Article 3, are additional penalised when there is absolutely no awareness. I can't really think about such a scenario where a person would not know that there is such an armed conflict, but it might be. And therefore, I tried desperately in the evening yesterday to find out what is the reason that brings you to the conclusion that when you find a person guilty, that he need not know about one element of crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I can just refer, if I may, to the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement. Sorry, I'm trying to find the exact passage. My recollection is that the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement, the Appellant argued that the -- the Appellant in that case, General Blaskic, had to know that the persons were protected persons, that actually he had to have the mental awareness of the fact that they were protected persons for compliance -- for liability under Article 2 charges. And that was raised and it was summarised in the Blaskic judgement as the position of the Appellant. And the subsequent findings of the Appeals Chamber in my submission concluded that it was not an element, it was not a mental element requirement that they actually -- that the accused is aware of the status of the protected persons. In my submission that's one example where this court, when raised specifically and it's summarised and I apologise, I'll get the reference to make sure I understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You need not. I looked it up yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I could have -- I should have assumed as much, Your Honour. But in that case, when it was raised specifically as a requirement under the Geneva Conventions and therefore a requirement in relation to the mens rea element, this Court did not accept that submission and found the Article 2 charges on the basis of the objective criteria. Now, therefore, we have Celebici, Tadic and specifically addressed in Blaskic where for those objective elements of the international armed conflict it was not found. Lastly I acknowledge that the ICC has taken a different point of view and I accept your proposition that in fact that there is knowledge of an armed conflict and that in most cases, be it international or non-international, it would be presumably relatively straightforward issue to address. And I also recognise that the state parties to the ICC have taken the position that that is a mental element and that, as a result, you do need to at least demonstrate an awareness of some of those elements even if they are classified as contextual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But finally, would it be your proposition in the unlikely event that an accused is not aware that there is such an armed conflict because the war -- the armed conflict just started that very moment, and he has no contact by media or whatsoever, he commits this crime, he's not aware that there is such an armed conflict, that then this crime is not only covered by other Articles or by other offences but even though he didn't know at all that there was an armed conflict, it arises -- it demands to additional to an article 2 crime, it would be the only -- sorry to ask you again, would you know about any crime where a perpetrator need not at least be aware of -- that there is such an element being the prerequisite of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If the Court determines that it is a requisite element of the crime as an element of mens rea, unlike the determinations for protected persons in Blaskic, then I would agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I follow with a brief question along the lines of my colleague, Judge Schomburg. Would you take your submissions as far as to challenge the proposition by the Trial Chamber that there must be a nexus between the act of the accused and the international armed conflict? The Trial Chamber referred to that in paragraph 176 when it says that the applicability of Article 2 of the Statute is subject to four prerequisites and first one was an armed conflict must exist; the second one, there must be a nexus between this conflict and the crimes charged. And then in paragraph 177, the last sentence, the Trial Chamber said, "The existence of an armed conflict nexus is established if the alleged crimes were closely related to the hostilities." Now, the question which I want to ask you is: How can it be determined that the act of the accused was closely related to the hostilities unless you take into account the mental state of the perpetrator of the act? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The way I interpret the -- that passage, if I may, Your Honour, in the way it's been interpreted in Celebici and Tadic is that it's an objective determination as to whether or not there is objectively a nexus to the armed conflict. I think this Court in Rutaganda dealt with that issue -- not with that specific issue, Your Honour, but dealt with whether or not the acts of the accused Rutaganda in that case were, whether there was a nexus and my recollection was that that was an objective nexus. In relation to whether or not there has to be a nexus between the armed conflict in the sense that it's an international armed conflict, I would submit there has to be a nexus with the armed conflict, with an armed conflict or the armed conflict, and then the determination of whether it's international or non-international would be an objective determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You're saying then by use of the word "objective" I understand you to be saying that the accused need not be shown to have any awareness of the existence of the international armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you like to turn your fertile mind to Article 3 of the Statute which relates to war crimes? I think that there is a requirement there to show that the particular war crime or alleged war crime was closely related to the armed conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How do you do that unless you show in some way not that the accused was participating in the armed conflict, or the international armed conflict in the case of Article 2, but that he knew of the existence of that conflict and that he -- he had that in mind when he committed the alleged crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, he had the armed conflict in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd have to check the case law to determine whether or not there has been a subjective requirement. My recollection, but I stand to be corrected of course, Your Honour, is that it's an objective requirement as to whether or not there is a nexus. But I would accept for the purposes of the proposition that you put, that he has to be aware that he's committing a crime in the context of, and it can't be the case that he thinks he's committing a domestic crime in the context of some type of local skirmish and not realising that he's taking -- it's taking place in a broader context but I don't think he has to actually be aware of the nature, extent, or involvement of troops and the conflict itself. He just has to know that there is something rising to a level of some form of conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do bear one thing in mind, Mr. Farrell. I might well have been engaged in some of these cases which are under review today but that does not prevent me from objectively considering the matter in the light of your submissions and those of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell you may continue your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There are three main issues that were raised by the Appellant, Mr. Martinovic, yesterday, that remain to be addressed. One was the murder of Mr. Nenad Harmandzic, the second was the wooden rifle incidents, and the third was the indictment issue and for which the Court asked questions of the Prosecution and of the Appellant. The fourth issue that was raised which we will not address but be available for questions is the issue of cumulative convictions. In light of the time I will be addressing if I can just outline where we will go in the next 40 minutes or so, I will address the murder of Nenad Harmandzic. Ms. Kind will address the issue of the wooden rifles, and then Mr. Kremer, as he addressed the issue of the indictment in relation to Mr. Naletilic, he will be available to address the issue of the indictment in relation to Mr. Martinovic. In light of the shortness of time I'm going to truncate all my submissions on the murder of Nenad Harmandzic. I think it's fairly well briefed. There is only one issue I will address, then, in a minute or two which is simply the difference between the expert opinions in relation to the identification of the body of Mr. Harmandzic. In summary form, there were two witnesses that were called, one by the Prosecution and one by the Defence. They disagreed on the manner in which the body was to be measured. One, the Defence expert, looked at the length of the bone and then calculated body height. The Prosecution expert looked at the length of the skeleton and then added centimetres for the living height. They came to different numbers. The Defence expert came to a range of 182 to 183. Plus or minus a margin of error of two which would make it somewhere in the range of 185 and that's where the questions stemmed from to the Prosecution expert as to whether he would agree to a margin of error of ten. As my friend said -- I think it was 11 to 14 as put by my friend. It's not 11 to 14. Even on the Defence expert it was 182, 183 plus a margin of error of 1 to 2 which made it 185 and because the Defence expert said 185 then the question to the Prosecution expert was, well, if it's 196 that's a big discrepancy. The Prosecution expert said 182 do 183 plus or minus a margin error of 2 for bone structure. That raised it to 815. Then the Prosecution expert said you had to add five centimetres on for the living height in addition to the skeletal height. That made it 190 for the Prosecution expert. Then there was extensive discussion about whether or not there could be a margin of error beyond that and whether or not that margin of error was such that would render the identification unreliable. This is where the divergence in the experts got greater. They were at different numbers, 185 and 190 and then at that point in time questions were asked as to whether or not that would be determinative. For the Defence expert, who stayed at 185, it was determinative. For the Prosecution expert, who came to the range of 190, the height of 196 was not determinative in terms of the identification of the body. I respectfully submit that the Trial Chamber was well within its authority to accept the testimony of one expert over the other and didn't enter into the recommend of providing expert opinion itself. In the questions put to the Defence expert, the Defence expert first of all acknowledged that the Prosecution expert, Dr. Zujo is an absolute expert. That were the words -- those were the words. He also explained that, in a question by Judge Clark, that it's not an absolute science. In fact he says it was based on calculations and population studies. The Defence expert admits that there can be a margin of error but concludes that the margin of error was different. And lastly the Court noted that the actual height of the victim was the approximation by the son. It was never scientifically established that he was 196 centimetres and in fact the Defence expert at transcript 14912 when asked about the height said, "The height came from the family. It's purely an impression and it's subjective." Judge Clark in the questions at transcript 7742, derives from the questions and answers by the Prosecution expert that it's only one factor and the Prosecution expert took the opinion that it is only one factor and that in light of the overwhelming evidence of the identifying features on the body itself, including the 6.35 calibre bullet which was found on the body of the decreased and the evidence given before the deceased was exhumed, that the person Nenad Harmandzic had shot himself in the leg with a 6.35 calibre bullet that very same bullet found in the vicinity of the right upper -- the right thigh. The age, the teeth, the injuries, the shoe size, the buckle, the lighter, the clothes, the blue blanket they were find -- found, and the fact that there was only one shoe, all these factors quite frankly in the Prosecution's submission are overwhelming and the difference between the Prosecution expert and the Defence expert was not a matter which would overturn the Trial Chamber's ultimate determination which in our submission was clearly within their realm to do. I won't address the issue of the documents or the testimony of Witness Ajanjic. We've set out in our brief our submission on those. I don't need to reiterate it in light of the time, unless there are questions on that particular -- those particular submissions. I'm sorry. I'll allow Ms. Kind to deal with the wooden rifle incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will respond to the submissions made by the Appellant Martinovic yesterday regarding the so-called wooden rifles incident for which the Appellant Martinovic was convicted for unlawful labour, inhumane acts, inhuman treatment, and cruel treatment. These are counts 2, 3, 4 and 5. The Appellant Martinovic alleged several errors by the Trial Chamber that led to his conviction for the use of four detainees from the Heliodrom detention facility as human shields on 17 September 1993. I generally refer to the Prosecution's response brief at paragraphs 3.16 to 3.27 and will today only address three of the allegations made yesterday, namely first the alleged recording of the return of the prisoners to the Heliodrom in Exhibit PP601.1. Secondly, the alleged inconsistencies in the evidence of the three victims who testified. And thirdly, the alleged involvement of secret police in the discovery of one of the wooden rifles. Turning to the first issue, the Appellant Martinovic asserts that all prisoners signed out from the Heliodrom detention facility by Vinko Martinovic on the 17th of September 1993 were returned to the Heliodrom by 27th September, including the four prisoners involved in the wooden rifles incident. And for this, the Appellant relies on Exhibit PP601.1, the Heliodrom logbook at page 01535273. I would now like to ask Your Honours and our learned friends to please look at the two relevant pages from Exhibit PP601.1, which should now come up on your screens. If you press the button computer evidence ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have no button.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: It's there, okay. Sorry. My technological knowledge is a bit limited. The relevant pages 01535272 and 01535273. On the first page you see the column on the right-hand side the list of names of detainees signed out to Vinko Martinovic on 17 September 1993. And then on page -- on the next page, 01535273, it continues, this list, at the left top corner. At the end, there, it says returned on 27 September 1993 at 1940 hours. I would now like to show you the translation of this part. First, the translation of the first page 01535272 at the bottom of this page, and then following over, the continuation and there you should be able to see the date and the time 27 September, returned at 1940 hours. Thank you. Now going back to the original B/C/S version, you will see that some of the names are ticked off while others have a small horizontal line next to them. The evidence shows that these horizontal lines are next to names of prisoners who were not returned to the Heliodrom. For example, the names of the four victims whose names are on this list and who testified before the Trial Chamber, Witnesses OO, J and PP. In order to be able to refer Your Honours to the names of these three witnesses, I would like to ask that we could briefly move into private session in order to protect the identity of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The evidence further shows that three other detainees listed here as signed out to Vinko Martinovic on 17 September 1993 did not return to the Heliodrom because they were killed on 17 September at the Bulevar confrontation line. They also have the small horizontal line next to their names. These are numbers 13, Hamdija Colakovic, number 19, Enes Pajo, and number 28, Aziz Colakovic. The death certificates of these three men were admitted into evidence as exhibits PP829 for Hamdija Colakovic, Exhibit PP849, Enes Pajo, and PP55, Aziz Colakovic. The Prosecution submits that in light of this evidence, it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to reject the Defence case that all prisoners were returned to the Heliodrom by 27 September 1993. I would now like to just briefly touch upon the two other issues raised yesterday. The first one, the alleged inconsistencies in the evidence of the three victims of the incident. The Prosecution submits that the testimonies of Witnesses OO, J, and PP were consistent in all material aspects, such as the names of the respective other three victims, how they were fetched from the Heliodrom early in the morning by Dinko Knezovic, a subordinate of Vinko Martinovic, and taken to Martinovic's headquarters. That Martinovic gave them the instructions to run across the confrontation line, the camouflage uniform they were given, the back packs full of stones, as well as the plastic bottles that were to look like Motorolas, how they had to move from the health centre towards the Bulevar next to the tank and run for their lives across the confrontation line. The Witness PP got seriously wounded but was pulled to safety. The Prosecution submits that in light of this it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to rely on the evidence of these three witnesses that was confirmed by other evidence in the case. And lastly regarding the allegations of the involvement of secret police in the discovery of one of the wooden rifles, the Prosecution submits that first of all, these allegations are wholly unfounded. The Prosecution invites the Defence to point to the evidence to actually support this claim. Secondly, the arguments are irrelevant because the Trial Chamber did not admit the wooden rifle which was tendered as Exhibit PP962 and the Trial Chamber considered this exhibit and rejected it at paragraph 287 of the judgement. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions on this topic. Unless there are questions I will just say a few words about sentencing and then pass on to Mr. Kremer. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: Just a few words regarding the issues raised yesterday. We rely on your our brief first of all but regarding the mitigating circumstances, voluntary surrender was raised. The Prosecution's position is that it was within the Trial Chamber's discretion not to accept the circumstances of Martinovic's transfer to The Hague as a mitigating factor and not to give them any weight. The Trial Chamber had specifically invited both parties for additional submissions on this topic in its order of 14 February 2003, and considered the circumstances of his transfer in paragraph 761 of the judgement and for more details, I refer Your Honours to paragraphs 9.2 to 9.14 of our brief and in particular paragraph 9.6. Regarding the argument that Mr. Martinovic assisted Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only one factual question. Does the Prosecution concede that the points made by the Defence yesterday that the Appellant tried his very best, being incarcerated in former Yugoslavia, to come immediately to The Hague and that he waived his right to appeal against the extradition decision and that it was the Prosecution hindering -- the Prosecution in Croatia hindering him in not coming immediately to the Tribunal so that finally he at least made some attempts to come to The Hague of his own? Is this factual -- is this a factual basis you would accept?

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: The Prosecution certainly accepts this factual basis. However, we would also like to refer you to your submissions in particular in paragraph 9.6 where we set out also some of the motives why Mr. Martinovic wanted to come to The Hague and we refer there to a statement that he made at the state court in Zagreb that he wanted to be transferred to The Hague to be retried for what he had been convicted for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the state court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KIND
utterances.text: With regard to the argument that Mr. Martinovic assisted Bosnian Muslims, the Prosecution's position is set out in paragraphs 9.15 to 9.18 in the brief. The issue was fully litigated at trial after the Trial Chamber had invited the parties to make specific submissions on this topic. The Prosecution submits it was within the Trial Chamber's discretion in light of the gravity of the crimes and Mr. Martinovic's active participation in a position of authority not to find that his assistance to a selected group of friends and neighbours was to be given any weight in mitigation. Regarding the aggravating circumstances, the Prosecution's position is that the Trial Chamber did not abuse its discretion by considering Martinovic's command role as an aggravating factor. In paragraph 758, the Trial Chamber first addressed issue of the gravity of the offence and found that although Mr. Martinovic did not have a significant -- sorry, yes. I apologise. Yes. That because he did -- although he did not have a significant role in the context of the wider conflict, his criminal conduct and the nature of the crimes in which he participated were of grave significance. And it then proceeded within the same paragraph to consider the fact that in his role as a subordinate to his soldiers he was respected and was in a position to influence the behaviour of the men in his unit and considered that in aggravation. Lastly with regard to the argument that the sentence is unfair compared to sentences received by other accused in this Tribunal, the Prosecution respectfully refers Your Honours to its response to Martinovic's supplemental appeal brief filed on 4 March 2005. And that concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kind. Yes, Mr. Kremer you may continue your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will not repeat the submissions in respect of our basic position responding to the vague indictment issue to the extent that I made reference to some background yesterday. I will focus principally on the general allegations made by Mr. Martinovic's counsel yesterday. I can say by way of starting that the complaints put forward before this Chamber were no different than he put forward before the Trial Chamber at the commencement of the proceeding, and in a disclose -- in a decision dated February 15th 2000, the Trial Chamber in responding to his complaint about the indictment, in particular the vagueness of the indictment, set out for him a road map as to what he should do to remedy the complaint to the extent that he felt that the allegations in the indictment were insufficient. The first tip that the Trial Chamber gave to Mr. Martinovic's counsel was to read the statements that he had been given. During the course of the motion, it was clear that Mr. Martinovic's counsel had not read all of the 137 witness statements that he had been given and the Court rightly pointed out that he should do so before making a complaint as to not knowing how or what to defend himself against. Secondly, the Court suggested that if Mr. Martinovic had a problem with the details surrounding the specifics of an indictment count, in particular an indictment count that offered only broad descriptions of the offences because of the systematic and long period of time over which the crime was taking place, then he should ask for particulars of the specifics from the Prosecution. Failing that, the Court also suggested that a demand for particulars could be filed with the Court. Mr. Martinovic's counsel did neither of those. He neither demanded or requested from the Prosecution particulars. He didn't make a demand for particulars. And the Prosecution did its utmost to provide Mr. Martinovic's counsel with information that would help him identify the particulars in respect of the general counts so that he could properly defend himself. I referred yesterday to the 65 ter list, and all of the witnesses that are relied on by the Trial Chamber find their way it on to a 65 ter list, one of the three that is filed as part of the pre-trial proceedings. I'm just going to refer to two witnesses because much focus yesterday was put on the unlawful transfer incidents, and Witness AB, for example - and if this Chamber goes to the witness list, the name of the witness can be identified - Witness AB testified -- says, according to the summary on the 65 ter list, on 19 July, 1993, his family was expelled from their apartment by Dario Solaja, the witness then describes that he's imprisoned in the Heliodrom, and he goes on to say at the end of the summary the witness was forced by Martinovic's men to loot Bosniak apartments. Looting was systematic and Martinovic was one of the chief organisers of the looting. He was present when goods were looted on to trucks. The witness also knew Kemo Selmanovic, a member of Tuta's unit who organised the expulsion of Muslims from Mostar and looting their property. Now specifically referred to as this witness, although he talks about the expulsions, is count 21, paragraph 57, which is the looting count. So there was information about looting. And another one about looting and then I'll get into the specifics of the two unlawful transfer counts, Witness II, in early August 1993 the witness was brought to Martinovic's headquarters near the Rondo where he performed different tasks. At the end of the summary, the witness was taken to assist in the looting of houses. Every day Stela's unit used 30 prisoners, ten for looting, ten for the front line, and ten to work at the headquarters. Stela was aware all of this was happening. The witness heard that his friends was forced to wear uniforms and carry wooden rifles on Stela's part of the confrontation line. So again, in terms of looting, he was put on notice as to Stela's involvement in looting and what witnesses were to testify about it. In terms of the unlawful transfer events, the witness Jeremy Bowen who was a video journalist took images that he filmed in the Mostar area during the month of September, in particular the day of September 29th and the early hours of September 30th, when a large segment of the population of Mostar was pushed across the river into the ABiH occupation zone or area. His transcript was disclosed in advance of his testimony. And prior to his testimony, a description of what he would be testifying about was set out by the Prosecutor and its relevance to the indictment. And this is so for all of the witnesses who testified before the Trial Chamber. Mr. Stringer points out at page 5767 of the transcript and also the evidence will be relevant to count 18 forced evictions, paragraph 24. The testimony of Witness GG at the beginning of the transcript, 4739, Mr. Poryvaev states "the witness is going to testify count 18, paragraph 54." At page 4756, the witness in answer to a question about being expelled, answers "I was again expelled from the apartment on June 13." And then he goes on at the next page to talk about the expulsion from his apartment and transfer on the 13th of June. It could not be any clearer. Witness WW, page 705, Mr. Scott introduces the witness as going to talk about count 18, paragraph 54. At paragraph 7006, I'm sorry, 7034, the witness talks about the 13th of June 1993. The witness is in fact directed by Mr. Scott to that date and asked to identify for the Court and describe what happened on that day and there is a fairly lengthy discussion about what took place on the 13th of June. That happens in respect of all of the witnesses. Now, if it wasn't enough that the witness statements put the accused on notice that these events were relevant to the indictment and were relevant to the particular counts in the indictment and the facts alleged in the indictment, there is more information disclosed to the accused from which he should have been put on notice. There is documentary evidence. And I'll just give a brief example because the Trial Chamber referred to much of this documentation in its judgement. P455.1 is a stamped daily report dated June 14, 1993 by Mate Anicic. For June 14th, 1993, HVO units under the command of Vinko Martinovic, aka Stela and 4Bat were performing ethnic cleansing. There is the videotape of the photo journalist I made reference to, Mr. Bowen, videotape Unfinished Business documentary of East Mostar by BBC correspondent Jeremy Bowen and again his testimony specifically mentions the 29th and 30th incident. And finally there is a report P620.1 and, as I say, there are many other documents that are disclosed prior to their introduction and during the course of the trial which clearly put Mr. Martinovic on notice as to the precise details, and these are just examples that are reflective of all of the counts that are in the indictment. It's a report to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Croatian Defence Council, and basically it's information, it's a military secret strictly confidential document to the Defence department, "abductions of Muslims from Centar II suburb on 29 September 1993. Around 1600 hours on September 29, 1993, Vinko Martinovic, aka Stela arrived at the Mostar Defence sector looking for the commander Miso Zelic. When he did not find him, he went to see Ivica Cavar at Sidi or aka Sidi, the deputy commander of the first light assault battalion and told him that the operation was to begin around 1900 hours in the evening as agreed." The last paragraph on the page. "It was agreed that two groups would conduct the operation, the Vinko Skrobo ATG, anti-terrorist group, and others. A plan was drawn up for the transfer of women and children to the left bank and men to Heliodrom to be kept for labour. The plan also envisaged seizing all apartment keys and placing stickers on apartment doors." It isn't any clearer that September 29th is a relevant date for the purposes of the indictment in terms of unlawful transfer of Muslim civilians of Mostar and similarly for June 13th and 14th. Plunder exhibits are -- or plunder examples and the beating examples all follow in the same fashion. There are various degrees of preciseness in the information. It's also supplemented by the specific statements of the witnesses that have been provided in advance, which -- in which more detail is given but our submission is that if there was a defect in the indictment in any way, it was cured by clear, concise, and timely information provided by the Prosecution during the course of its disclosure and pre-trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You already said when one comes to the conclusion that the indictment as such is not clear enough when it reads for example in para 27, "however, there were two large waves of forcible transfers and imprisonment, one in the days following the 9 May 1993 attack and the second during the first days of July 1993." One could arguably say that this is too vague and it covers -- does not cover the 29 September. What would you see as curing, if at all, the vagueness of the indictment? The 65 ter list, the statements given, or something we are very familiar with in both major legal systems, the judicial hint given at trial? As you referred to, what would you finally say is the final act curing a possible vagueness of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The final act? They are -- all of the circumstances. The initial guidance provided by the Trial Chamber as to what Mr. Martinovic and his counsel should do to provide or to obtain the particulars that they were seeking, the provision of the information pursuant to 65 ter, the immediate cross-reference given the names of the witnesses that the crown had -- or the Prosecution had identified as their witnesses to be called at trial, by reference to the statement that is were previously disclosed, the reference to documents that dealt with the same incidents because the 65 ter list identified particularly the specific incidents that the witness would be speaking to and connected it to a paragraph and count in the indictment, the fact that the witness was called to testify and was identified prior to his testimony by the Prosecution as going to testify about a specific paragraph and count, the fact that the witness did testify, the fact that the witness was cross-examined, that there was no objection to the witness testifying as to that account because the Defence was being taken by surprise, there was none of that. There was actually cross-examination. So that the combination of what the events when looked at retrospectively confirm that there was no unfairness and ultimately the question is: Even if the indictment is vague, that vagueness was cured during the course of the trial such that it has not been demonstrated by Mr. Martinovic that he received an unfair trial, that the incidents on which the conviction was based were clearly informed or were clearly made aware to him through the various disclosure in advance of the witness testimony. He wasn't surprised when they testified because he had been given the documents. He had been given the witness statements, he had been given the 65 ter notice, and he had the indictment which provided the details of the between dates of this conduct, the conduct of plunder, the conduct of beatings, the conduct of forcible transfer. There were many, many, many incidents and the Court chose to look at precise incidents which were components of the more general charge. And the more general charge was required because of the nature and number of the incidents that took place. And so it fell to the Prosecution to provide information to the Defence in the 65 ter list and in the statements and in the documents and the Defence had the opportunity, if it was confused to ask, and it chose not to -- to bring a motion for particulars, it chose not to. And our position is that in order to make a valid argument before this Chamber it must be demonstrated that there is an unfairness worked against the accused because of the lack of clear, concise, and timely information. There has been no such showing. In fact I would submit, based on my submissions, it's the opposite. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, is this Bench entitled to draw any inferences from the fact, as you assert, A, that the Trial Chamber indicated to the Defence the possibility of the Defence asking for particulars, and, B, the fact that the Defence did not ask for particulars? Is this Bench entitled to draw any inferences as to whether the Defence was really embarrassed or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think it's entitled to take that fact into account in determining whether there has been any prejudice at the trial. That's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I understand there are no more questions by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the question of alternative and cumulative charging, Mr. Tracol is here to answer any questions since it was raised in the Court's letter and scheduling order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I don't think there is any questions. So this concludes the response of the Prosecution. Now we will turn to counsel for Martinovic for their reply. They have 30 minutes for the reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I will try to briefly turn to all the issues raised by the Prosecution and I hope that I will be able to give the floor then to my colleague, Kerns, to address some of the legal matters before the Tribunal. Let us start from the end of my learned colleague's submissions as to the vagueness of the indictment. The position of the Defence is as follows: The accused has the right to be served a clear indictment. This is a matter that he is entitled to from day 1, without any reservations. This is one of his fundamental rights and that's the position of the Defence, and he claims that right this -- today as well. The -- we heard the Prosecutor today say that the Defence counsel were given guidance by the Trial Chamber. Guidance about what? To draft an indictment for ourselves? The Chamber said that we had witness statements, we had different lists to see for ourselves what the charges were about. What were we supposed to do then? To draft the charges ourselves? Well, I think I can go only this far in saying what our position is in relation to the indictment. As for the wooden rifles incident, my learned colleague came up with a list of who was alive, who was returned and who was not. I have one question to raise in this relation. We have mentioned several persons who were killed on that list but Mr. Martinovic was convicted on that count. However they were killed elsewhere. It is our submission that they were killed because they were holding wooden rifles in a different unit. On the issue of Harmandzic's murder and whether it was a murder or not, I submit respectfully that this Chamber should look at how the OTP alternatively charged this incident. Now, why was it charged in this particular fashion? It wasn't a coincidence. It was charged both as murder and cruel treatment in order to cover all bases. We know beyond any dispute that Harmandzic was in Martinovic's unit. Now, whether he was beaten there or not is open for discussion. Now, why was it charged this way by the OTP? Well, in order to make sure that they cannot lose this battle, and I am shocked to this day that the Trial Chamber accepted this bait offered by the OTP and I respectfully submit that the Appeals Chamber should regard this issue from this perspective as well. The international armed conflict was presented to us from the perspective of the OTP, and my learned colleague Farrell. Now, where is Martinovic's subjective position in relation to this conflict? What my learned colleague said simply doesn't stand. They offered to us the Danish cook, Allen Knudsen. They told us to look at the paragraphs in the judgement. I tell you to look at the transcript. This was a very intelligent young man, a very dangerous man who could not be confused easily. He told us that he had been working as a cook in Denmark. He was an adventurer who wanted to wage a war. He found an advert in the papers where they were recruiting people for wars in Croatia, Afghanistan, Iraq. He arrived in Croatia. He had a phone number that he had to call; that was the only thing he had this his hand when he left Denmark. He was told to report to someone at the main railway station in Zagreb upon his arrival there. There was a group of them there who were met by this man Brajcic, whatever his name was, who was recruiting volunteers. He wasn't doing it on behalf of the Croatian government. This man Knudsen could have reported in Canada or anywhere else, wherever there were people recruiting volunteers for wars. Therefore, this was a person who had nothing to do with the Croatian state. Allegedly he was taken to the Croatian parliament. No, he was taken to the canteen in the Croatian parliament because that's where he worked. And from there, he was sent to Mostar, and he was carrying papers. Why? Well, because they had to make sure that he wasn't killed upon his arrival in Mostar because he could have been mistaken for a spy. My client Martinovic does not recall the paper itself but, of course, the person had to have some papers on him in order to identify himself. And it is on the basis of this particular document that we should take decisions relevant for international law as to Martinovic's awareness or less? Now, on the basis of the testimony of this Allen Knudsen person we should judge Martinovic's responsibility? This example could serve more to prove Denmark's awareness of the international armed conflict rather than Martinovic's. I would only like to draw one parallel in this respect. What is the Prosecutor's intention in referring to Knudsen? They wish to discredit the testimony of Martin Garrod. We know who this person was. He was the chief of the monitoring mission in Mostar at the time who visited Martinovic's headquarters on a daily basis. He knew what was going on in Mostar. Whenever he sent out a report, the capitals throughout the world would be calling back on the basis of his reports. And he was the person who testified to the matter of the international armed conflict, and when he was testifying before the Trial Chamber here, he was asked on this issue of the subjective approach to the international armed conflict, suddenly the OTP finds this to be a ridiculous issue. Martin Garrod was asked as to whether he knew Martinovic. He said that he did because he met him on a daily basis. He was asked about the role that Martinovic had, about what kind of strategic information he might have had at the time. Look at the testimony by Martin Garrod on page 8595, when he was asked about Martinovic's awareness or participation in the international armed conflict. He was the person who was best placed to answer such a question, and his answer was that it was impossible for him to have such information. The only thing he was concerned with was to survive. And it was this Danish cook, the other witness, who was supposed to discredit a witness of such -- whose testimony had such weight. And that would be all I would have to submit on this matter. My colleague, Mr. Kerns, will address you on the matter of the international armed conflict and other legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: May it please the Court, counsel, I wanted to take some time this morning to brought up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: -- by my learned friend Mr. Farrell yesterday. In his opening remarks he seemed to suggest to this Court that this issue of mens rea as it relates to international armed conflict I believe his words were: It wasn't briefed. So he kind of suggested to this Court that, well, we should be able to supplement our briefing. What he meant by that was we didn't respond to the Defence's argument on this issue so we would like an additional opportunity to brief. I want to draw the Court's attention to -- specifically to our very first ground of appeal stated in the appellate brief my counsel, Mr. Par, drafted. And under the ground stated first ground of appeals errors of law right at paragraph 8 and 9 it reads as follows: That "Mr. Martinovic cannot be held responsible for the character of the armed conflict in which he found himself in the period relevant to the indictment. In particular, the character of the armed conflict is beyond his knowledge and awareness and intention. It was indisputable that Mr. Martinovic was positioned in front of his house in Mostar, on a street 200 metres long. "First he was there in defence of the Serb forces in 1992 and second when he was there when the Muslim forces attacked in 1993. "Mr. Martinovic had no connection with persons, authorities, units, outside of Mostar and had no way of knowing this wider context." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel you have to slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours. My point being that when my learned colleague suggested, well, at least inferred that this is somehow a new issue that just got raised on the first day of oral argument, it's not the case. It was briefed in our very first issue, very first ground of law, and then you'll note that we filed a supplemental brief which specifically cited the Kordic appeal. Not only that, the Prosecution responded by filing a separate response to our supplemental brief, again they cited the Kordic appeal. So it's somewhat disingenuous to say that, now paragraph 311 of the Kordic appeal has taken us off guard and we need an opportunity to brief this issue on the second day of oral argument. I also note my learned colleague Mr. Hennessy sought weeks ago to file supplemental arguments on the issue of torture and, of course, this Court in its discretion said, hey, the time for drafting supplemental arguments is passed. The oral argument stage is at hand and now my learned colleague says we need another opportunity to try to convince the Kordic Appeal Chamber it's wrong as to this issue of mens rea. When -- our point being that when we were citing Kordic in February of this year, when the Prosecutor was citing Kordic in March of this year, it's somewhat disingenuous to come before this Chamber and say, well, we would like to opportunity to further brief the issues in core different which, by the way, was decided in December of last year. Why are they saying this? They are saying it because that hurts our position. We didn't respond at all, frankly, to the issues raised by the Defence at the time. We didn't come before the Chamber either through brief or otherwise until Mr. Farrell stood up yesterday to try and point out these facts that supposedly substantiate my client's mens rea. Which I think a full reading of the transcript will establish there was none. This is a man that the Trial Chamber described as a Mostar boy, who was raised in Mostar, stayed in Mostar, fought on a very small front line in Mostar, that if you are a decent golfer you could hit a golf ball and cover his entire area of responsibility. They wanted to infer that by -- there was men with HV uniforms around. The Court -- the Trial Chamber also found that of course there were going to be men with HV uniforms because many Bosnian Croats went to Croatia to fight and then returned when the war came to Mostar. So the existence of uniforms is proof of nothing, as to my client's mens rea. So I would like to ask this Honourable Court to look at those arguments of the counsel with a little bit of suspicion when they say we are surprised by paragraph 311 that says there is a mens rea requirement. As the Honourable Judge Schomburg mentioned, they weren't even able to point to a single case in any country of the world that says that an element of a crime can just be imputed or inferred. Counsel suggested because of the mens rea requirement wasn't really raised in Kordic and in Tadic, that these are somehow overruled -- I'm sorry, in Tadic and Cerkez that they are somehow overruled by Kordic. The fact that the issue wasn't raised, the logic then doesn't follow that that issue was somehow overruled by Kordic when the issue wasn't even discussed. The lawyers didn't even raise the issue as we have, specifically in paragraphs 8 and 9 of our brief. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It isn't the Defence's fault frankly, it isn't Mr. Martinovic's fault, that no other lawyers decided to raise this issue in those other cases. We very specifically raised that issue and I would like to -- and I'll address you more on that. This morning, counsel for the Prosecution argued, well, the nexus is also an objective test. Not only is the nexus an objective test but the very existence of an international armed conflict is also an objective test. Everything seems to be an objective test where we don't look at my client's state of mind being a man who is raised in Mostar, stayed in Mostar, fought in Mostar against the Serbs, originally fought alongside the Muslims, then later fought against the Muslims, all in a single front line area. That's the context for which they now come before this Court and argue there is proof beyond all reasonable doubt that he must have known that this was international in nature. Remember that the trial court described him as a local boy with a basic education and no military training whatsoever, a taxi driver who became well respected and became commander of a very small unit along the front line. The Kordic opinion specifically stated that a person -- a soldier must be aware at least of the factual circumstances, at least that a foreign state was involved. In this armed conflict, and as my learned colleague Mr. Par just mentioned, what did the witness state as to my client's knowledge? It was simply we were thinking about keeping our heads on our shoulders. We are on the front line. We are worried about surviving from the guys shouting-distance away. The Trial Chamber found he had zero political connections whatsoever. We are talking about a very small role that Mr. Martinovic played in this incident. Your Honours, I would -- I know that my learned friend Mr. Farrell did give Mr. Naletilic sometime to respond because they were kind of tangentially raised, but I did want to bring that issue before the Court and I'll be back before you after Mr. Farrell talks again. And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Am I assuming that this concludes your reply, Mr. Kerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: For this phase, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, according to our schedule, we would break now and then start with the Prosecutor's appeal after the break. Mr. Farrell?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Just on one excuse me Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. Just -- I don't want to prejudge Mr. Naletilic. Maybe he has no submissions to make but in light of the fact that did I raise factual matters yesterday on the international armed conflict, on the knowledge of Mr. Naletilic, that's the only issue that I had left open, just in relation to the starting time or, I'm sorry, the starting of the Prosecution appeal next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Farrell. I simply had no request from the Defence of Mr. Naletilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour, and I leave it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hennessy?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: If it's all right with the Court, I'll visit with my co-counsel and we will decide whether to make any further submissions about international armed conflict during the time previously allotted to us which I believe begins at noon today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You mean you would like to make submissions in responding to the Prosecution appeal? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Well, I would be happy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We would conclude now the appeal of Martinovic, the appeal of Naletilic, it concluded yesterday. We should start with the Prosecution appeal. It's your -- it's your intention to make some further submission on behalf of Naletilic as to the armed conflict in responding to the Prosecution? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Let me say I don't expect to have any further response with respect to international armed conflict, but if this is an open invitation there were some remarks by Mr. Kremer regarding the sufficiency of the indictment that were not made in a time frame where I had the ability to respond and I do have a brief response to some of the specific, for example, the specific references to 65 ter production that I would like to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I understand that your submissions in the afternoon should be limited to the Prosecution -- responding to the Prosecution appeal. The time for the Naletilic appeal has expired now. That's how we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If you want to make some short remarks on the factual finding -- factual submission made yesterday by Mr. Farrell, as concerns the internationality of the conflict, I can give you ten minutes for that, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: As to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I would prefer to do it now, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: As to international armed conflict I have no submission for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: I was trying to be just as polite as I could to my counsel to give him a couple of minutes but I then do have two minutes of response with regard to the sufficiency of the indictment argues, maybe even a minute and 30 seconds, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You still would have until -- seven minutes for that. Please. Make use of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: My learned colleagues also made an argument -- Peter argued to this honourable court, look at all the warnings we gave in relation to this indictment. We told them they could file these documents. We told the Defence they could ask who for specifics. We called witnesses who said they were going to be talking about September 29. So how could they not know this defect has been cured? But also, I would ask this Court to recall that many times in the course of almost every trial, there is evidence as to motive, opportunity and intent, other bad acts of the accused which are not charged as crimes but they are offered as proof of motive, knowledge, intent, preparation, plan. In our federal courts in America it's referred to as Rule 404(b) evidence, other bad acts that tends to prove the facts in the indictment but they are not charged as crimes. Here, what my learned friend submits is, hey, we can throw in any bad act we want and then call it a crime at the end of the case when the Defence sits there and is looking through the indictment and saying well we are not even charged with it. There must be 404 B. It must be prior bad act evidence. Why are we worried about this? It's almost as if the Prosecution wants to say to this honourable Chamber, Anything bad they talk about your client, watch out, because it might also be a crime that you're charged with as well. How hard is it for one of them to -- they filed an amended indictment once. How hard would it have been to get on the word processor and type September 29th is charged as well? I would submit to you that it's not an onerous burden on the Prosecution to give sufficient notice of what an accused is charged with. Especially in light of the various jurisprudence that allows for courts to allow evidence of other bad acts in support of the acts that are charged. And that's the point that I wanted to share with the Court and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please Your Honour and I'm going to be really short but there were issues raised yesterday as to the vagueness of the indictment that we have not been able to address and I just then respectfully asking Your Honours if I may do that at noon for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, why have you not been able to address it yesterday? You could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have time yesterday and there were also factual issues brought up by Mr. Farrell regarding Simang, Falk, which I would like to respond to also but, you know, if you're going to take a break, that's fine, Your Honours, but in the interests of justice, I don't think that ten minutes is going to ruin anything or stop this train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, I already told you that I was ready to give ten minutes to address the question that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But Mr. Hennessy said that they have nothing to do. So you should make up your mind then on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That was -- that was-- excuse me, Your Honour. I make -- Mr. Hennessy indicated that he didn't have anything to say on international armed conflict, and I'm talking about the vagueness of the indictment as regards Mr. Naletilic. I'm asking for ten minutes at noon, Judge. That's all I'm asking for. In the interests of justice. Mr. Farrell? What is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Though I appreciate the concerns of Mr. Meek and I don't mean to be unfair in any way, but as the parties have been limited to the time period, it's my submission that if they chose to address other issues during their response that's of course their choice. Of course, we are not prejudiced in any way but, of course, I presume that all of us would like to make more submissions on a few other matters but that's not the purpose today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, having consulted my colleagues on the Bench, I will give you until 10.40, just to address new arguments made by the Prosecution. Ten minutes. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate this. Briefly I'm going to tell you that -- and I agree with what Mr. Kerns said that in the course of trials, when you're a trial lawyer you'll know that the evidence that comes in that may not be relevant to a count in the indictment. Let me tell you that if you look at the Defence for Naletilic's, our final brief, we never even addressed the issue of expulsions in June 13th and 14th or September 29th. Why? Because we didn't know we were charged with those crimes. We addressed everything, it's a 180-page final brief, but yet nothing on those issues because we were not given proper notice. In any trial, we all know this as lawyers and judges, in any trial, what is the first thing that happens? The Prosecutor gives an opening statement. That opening statement is to outline the evidence he intends to prove and introduce at trial in order to show hopefully proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused committed this crime, this crime, that crime, or this crime. Review the opening statement of Mr. Scott on September 10th, 2001, and Your Honours, he mentioned May 9 expulsions, and he mentioned July 30th. No mention is made of 13, 14 June, no mention is made of 29 September whatsoever. And for the Prosecution to say, well, you know, they were put on notice by witnesses that came and testified, they should have known that during the trial, that begs the question of whether a proper notice was given in the indictment. There has been cases from this Tribunal that very clearly say that if you have a case where there is too many victims, for example, to name them all, you don't have to. But if it's a simple case of typing in another sentence, such as, and also expulsions on 13, 14 June, 1993 in Mostar, and 29 September, 1993, in Mostar, that the Prosecutor should do that. It's just fundamental fairness, and my gosh, we did not even address this issue in our final brief and it wasn't because we missed anything, Your Honours. It's because we weren't put on notice until the judgement came down that Mr. Naletilic was even charged, even under 7(3) grounds, with those expulsions. And that is just fundamentally unfair. Read the opening statement and you will see what I mean. I would love, and, Judge, I've been closer than -- ten minutes, I think I've only used five, but I won't speak any more about Falk Simang and Ralf Mrachacz. I just ask you to read their testimonies and you'll see why they are so unbelievable that they should have been completely disregarded. And thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Well, we can break now for 30 minutes. We will reconvene at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: According to our schedule, we will now proceed to hear the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution will have one hour for its submissions and then we'll hear part of the response of Naletilic for 30 minutes before the lunch break. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. May -- just one point. My client has again asked me to inquire as to whether the Chamber has made a decision as to whether he might be able to speak longer than 15 minutes this afternoon, should Mr. Martinovic not take his whole 15 minutes. That's the only question I had for my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, the Chamber has made a determination. I think we'll give Mr. Naletilic five minutes more than the schedule of 20 minutes but this is not linked to Mr. Martinovic's using or not his time. Mr. Martinovic will still have 15 minutes to address the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We believe that's very fair. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So Mr. Kremer, you can proceed to your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I can inform the Chamber that I will deal with the deportation issue. My colleague, Mr. Farrell, will deal with the persecution, and Mr. Tracol will deal with the cumulative conviction issue in the Prosecution's notice of appeal. Just before we start, I'm not going to be referring at all to the Prosecution's appeal brief other than to point out that paragraph 4.7 or 4.8, I'm sorry, has a correction that is required. In the first sentence to paragraph 4.8, there is an omission which I believe is important and that should be pointed out so that there is no misunderstanding as to the position. The ordinary English language meaning of the word deportation is "the action of carrying away, forcible removal" - there were a few words omitted; I don't know why, because I didn't prepare the brief - "esp. into exile; transportation." I thought I would bring that to the Chamber's attention so that the reference to the English dictionary definition is complete. The position that we are advancing by way of oral argument is consistent with the position that we advanced in our written brief but it takes on a different approach and, I would submit, a more persuasive approach to the question as to how this Chamber should define the term "deportation" for the purposes of Article 5(D) of the Statute. We start from the underlying principle that unlawful displacement of a civilian population, whether described as unlawful transfer or deportation is a war crime and/or a crime against humanity under customary international law. And we say that the crime has been described as such since Nuremberg. Making displacements of a civilian population a crime protected fundamental human rights and this Chamber has acknowledged in the Krnojelac decision the protected right I am speaking of at paragraph 218. It said "the prohibition against forcible displacement of people aims at safeguarding the right of individuals to live in their communities and homes without interference. The forced character of displacement and forced uprooting of inhabitants of a territory entail the criminal responsibility of the perpetrator, not," and I emphasise the word not, "the destination to which these inhabitants are sent." This Chamber also in Krnojelac discussed both crimes using the label forcible displacement and decided that the act of displacing civilians was the underlying act in the crime against humanity of persecution under Article 5(H). Regardless of whether the act resulted in a transfer to a place within the territory or to another country. For discussion purposes this morning, I will use the label unlawful displacements but point out that the terms deportation and forcible transfers are more commonly used in indictments before this Tribunal. The Prosecution agrees with the Appeal Chamber Krnojelac decision that the conviction for the crime of persecution was justified in this case as the underlying act of unlawful displacement had been established. That takes us to the question that the Appeals Chamber appears to be interested in, and that is how should deportation be defined for the purposes of Article 5(D) of the Statute. Our position is with respect that deportation includes unlawful or forcible transfer. The Appeals Chamber settled the law applicable to crime against humanity of Prosecution and it remains for it to classify under which crime against humanity unlawful displacement falls, whether labelled deportation or unlawful or forcible transfer, when no discriminatory intent exists. In its appeal, the Prosecution submits that the Appeals Chamber's reasoning in Krnojelac applies especially to deportation as a crime against humanity. If the destination of the victims is irrelevant, to the definition of the crime in customary international law as this Chamber has found, then the definition of deportation in Article 5(D) can include all unlawful displacements, including forcible transfers or unlawful transfers, however you choose to define it. Customary international law supports this position. We have filed with the Chamber a supplementary book of authorities with the compilation of sources in relation to displacement and displaced persons from the International Committee of the Red Cross study on customary international humanitarian law published in 2005. Never before has such an extensive body of sources been available for interpreting customary international law and interpreting customary international law on this subject. This study, ten years in the making, shows that the language used to define the crime of displacement, albeit in the context of the laws of war and the customs of war, is not consistent and that a border is only infrequently included in the definition. If you look at the book of authorities, the chapter that has been filed with the Chamber, you will see that only 17 of the 243 sources in this chapter mention a transfer to another state. Nearly 200 mention occupied territory and 47 make no reference to occupied territory. A review of the sources demonstrates that the many terms -- that many terms are used to describe displacement as a crime. Unlawful transfer, illegal transfer, forcible transfer, forced displacement, unlawful displacement, forcible eviction, expulsion, mass expulsion, driving away of, deportation, and forced deportation. In many cases, two or more of these terms are used together to describe the crime. While the language lacks consistency, the underlying principle remains sacrosanct. That is, displacement of a civilian population is universally criminal. The Prosecution submits that a definition of deportation that includes unlawful or forcible transfer affirms the principle that unlawful displacement is a crime in customary international law and conforms to the practice of defining the crime at customary international law. This definition will provide a clear definition and direction to the Trial Chambers and to the parties. I infer from the questions posed in the scheduling order that I should be commenting about the two crime option. The Appeal Chamber has posed the question about the definition of deportation assuming inclusion of a border element. To answer this question, the Appeals Chamber must honour the underlying principle that I started my remarks with, that unlawful displacement of a civilian population, whether described as unlawful transfer or deportation, is both a war crime and a crime against humanity under customary international law. How can the Appeals Chamber describe the crime to include a border element or a destination of the displacement and honour the fundamental principle? Recognising a border element forces the recognition of two crimes. One carried out within the territory of the state and the other across its border. This can only be accomplished by defining unlawful displacement to another country as deportation, a crime against humanity under Article 5(D), and unlawful displacement within the territory as an other inhumane act as a crime against humanity under Article 5(I). While two separate crimes are recognised, and differentiated by destination of the transfer, the criminalisation of the conduct is preserved. The Appeals Chamber also asked a question involving de facto borders. Our research has not disclosed any customary international law support for the notion of a de facto border. Although territorial borders are used to differentiate between unlawful transfer and deportation in the war crimes context. Deportation and unlawful transfer protects against unlawful displacements against a national border and within the territory of the occupied state. The occupation does not change the manner in which this protection is applied. Although providing clear definition and direction to the Trial Chambers and the parties, this interpretation will conflict with definitional practices in defining the crime at customary international law to which I have referred the Chamber earlier. However, this approach raises one question which warrants brief review. Can forcible displacements be classified under other inhumane acts under Article 5(I)? This requires two determinations to be made. Are other inhumane acts crimes under -- crimes, under Article 5(I)? And do unlawful displacements within a territory meet the equal gravity test for other inhumane acts set out in the jurisprudence? The answer to the first question is yes. This Chamber in Krnojelac found that forcible displacements were the underlying crimes of persecution. At paragraph 223, the Chamber concluded displacements both within a state and across a national border were crimes under customary international law. Consequently, the principle nullum crimen sine lege has been respected. Nullum crimen sine lege is respected whether the crime of unlawful displacement at customary international law falls under persecution or other inhumane acts. The absence of discriminatory intent does not make the conduct any less a crime. This conclusion is supported by the Trial Chamber decisions in Krstic, paragraphs 520 to 523, Kupreskic, paragraphs 562 to 566, and Blagojevic, paragraph 625 to 630. Unlawful displacements were found in the Krnojelac appeal decision to be of equal gravity to other crimes listed in Article 5 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber stated at paragraph 221 that, "This analysis is also supported by recent state practice as reflected by the Rome Statute which provides that displacements both within a state and across national borders can constitute a crime against humanity and a war crime. The crime of unlawful displacement within a state must be classified within Article 5 of the Statute. If Article 5(D) deportation includes only the crime of unlawful displacement, across the border, then to avoid decriminalising the crime of unlawful displacement within a state, the crime must fall squarely within Article 5(I), 'other inhumane acts.'" Conclusion: The Appeals Chamber has two options. One, define deportation under 5(D) consistent with the customary international law including the ICC definition as including all unlawful displacements however described without regard to destination. Or, define deportation as an unlawful displacement across a national border and acknowledge that unlawful displacement within a -- the territory is another inhumane act. Either option provides certainty and clarity. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, I think we are all in agreement that we don't have a question of nullum crimen sine lege before us. It's only a question of a clear classification of the acts, and my question to you would be: Wouldn't it be helpful to make a clear distinction between a deportation across a border, we will come back to the question of de facto or de jure later, across a border or inside the territory? I think the rationale and the same gravity allows to have the latter one under 5(I), but when you approach Article 5 systematically, don't you have first to address the question are the prerequisites of 5(D) fulfilled before you come to the catchall crime in 5(I)? What is the rationale behind? I think both, and unfortunately we have slightly different version in English and in French, but what they have in common is the prefix a deportation or expulsion, meaning that you are deported, expelled from the territory where the state guarantees by its sovereignty your safety both in terms that you are not, say, illegally extradited, that there is a social net, and so on and so forth, that you are no longer under the shelter of your own state.
