Therefore I fully agree with you that the destination in fact is immaterial, but isn't it worthwhile to develop further international law departing -- I don't really know whether it's departing because we've -- we found that the indictment in Nuremberg, for example, clearly alleged deportation inside Germany, and so therefore the border seems to be not relevant for this definition at that time, but isn't it true that when interpreting a norm that you also have to take into account the real circumstances in the world? And don't they have changed? And isn't it true that it would be an advantage to have a clear definition that those acts of mopping up inside a country falls under forcible displacement or forcible transfer, whereas bringing a person over a border, this should be qualified clearly as deportation or expulsion, and as the destination is not -- is irrelevant, I think, for example, when you look on the map of Europe, how would you qualify a forcible transfer or deportation to Transdniestria? There is no border that's internationally recognised. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It's recognised by the Russian Federation and by Abkhazia. So would this be enough? Is it really necessary to find out today in a changed world that there is an international recognised border? Some scholars say it's very difficult to clarify what is a de facto border, whereas the -- how can we define it? But isn't it quite clear in this case? Several times, the judgement and already the indictment speaks about separation lines, Mostar divided, dividing Mostar. Indictment paragraph 53, across the confrontation line. Military front line, paragraph 23. So finally, wouldn't you agree that today the law has developed to that end that not the de jure border but a de facto border suffices because the rationale behind is in fact the same and only one point you have not addressed, that's the question of permanent displacement. I think in the definition also the mens rea element of permanent displacement should be included. May I please have your opinion on this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: First of all I would submit with respect that the submission that you just made on -- in favour of a de facto border is a policy argument not a legal argument. We are dealing here with a legal issue that must be interpreted by a court of law that must apply customary international law. The authorities that we have provided to the Chamber clearly demonstrate that a de facto border has no support, notwithstanding the changing political times, that the situation here obviously had a military confrontation line, it had what you would describe as a de facto border, but at international law, under the laws and customs of war in particular, it would not recognise the de facto border. And what our submission is based on primarily is that there has to be a recognition of the two crimes: The unlawful transfer within the state, which is recognised at customary international law in the Geneva Conventions and onward, and a deportation from a state. Our primary argument is based on the fact that over the last 60 years, the choice of words to describe these two types of conduct has become merged into a single concept, forced transfer, forced displacements, and the border has become irrelevant. And to the extent that this Chamber found that in the Krnojelac decision it properly interpreted customary international law. Our position moves from that and relies on the fact that the concepts are merged and that deportation can and should include the definition of forcible transfer within it, under Article 5(D) but the primary position that we start from is that there are -- there is one crime, that's a forced displacement, regardless of where the person ends up, and the principle has to be honoured. And if a de facto border is put into place, accepting that there is a 5(I) crime to deal with the internal transfers within the territory of the government that is doing the forcible displacing out of its territory, there is complete coverage, but that's not the question that needs to be addressed by this Chamber. The question that needs to be addressed is in looking -- in determining a border element, is it consistent with customary international law? And the authorities point to the fact that a territorial border or a border of occupation becomes relevant but the border of occupation does not change the definition of the term, whether it's within the territory or outside of the territory within the territory of the former state. It's only when the transfer is to another country under the laws of war does it become a deportation in the context of the Geneva Conventions. So our position is, as long as there is complete coverage, either under the two crime option or the single definition option, then international law has been honoured. If, as in the Stakic decision, there is a void in the law because 5(I) is decriminalised and there is no coverage within the territory of the occupier, then there is a problem, and so in answer to your question I would submit that a de facto border doesn't solve any problems; it probably creates more problems than it resolves because of the questions as to where was the confrontation line on a certain day? Is a confrontation line a territorial line? If a person is deported from Mostar to Zagreb and they are asked where did you get off the train, I was forced off the train in Zagreb, I think the Court can take judicial notice of the fact that they are in another country. The proof is simple. I hope I've answered your question. The other -- the permanent intent question, if there is no border requirement, then there is no mens rea requirement. Our position is that there -- that this Trial Chamber, this Tuta and Stela Trial Chamber, misinterpreted the provisions relating to evacuation. An evacuation makes a displacement lawful. It doesn't impose into it an interpretive definition that says that the transfer must be permanent. The intent that's required is that the person must know and intend that the person is being transferred from his home to another place. Where the person is going, how the person gets there, and whether the person can and will come back or is intended to come back by the people organising it is something that is not relevant. It's the participation, the ordering or participation in the physical transfer and relocation of these people that is the critical mental element that is all the crime requires.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney, you want to put a question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: You have just said that a de facto border cannot solve the problem, you said, and it maybe even source of conflict. What about generally recognised de facto borders, which is a concept followed in many cases under international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The International Court of Justice spends years trying to decide the borders of a state and borders are defined different ways, by treaty, by convention, by commissions and determinations by the International Court of Justice. A national border, if recognised, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Not only recognised but generally recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Generally recognised, has some issues to it, whether that's comparable to a de jure border is something that I would -- I would say is open to debate and whether a generally recognised border is sufficient for customary international law terms to supplant the concept of -- to the -- to another country becomes somewhat problematical. I think that a generally recognised or generally accepted border, and I would not say de facto border, I would say a generally accepted or generally recognised border, may well be equivalent to a de jure border. Depending on the definition. My problem in answering your question, with respect, is that I don't understand the concept of a generally accepted, whether it's -- generally accepted de facto border. I would say generally accepted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: De facto border generally accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I think that either we start from the -- the problem that de facto border cannot be defined. And is not defined at customary international law. A generally accepted border is. Whether it's de jure or generally accepted, I think that's the comparison, not the starting point being a de facto border, with all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Farrell, you may continue your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I will be dealing with the Prosecution's first ground of appeal, the ground of appeal dealing with persecutions. If I may just clarify Mr. President, I think we started sometime around between 5 and 10 after. I'll certainly try to be within the time frame of one hour, though I may ask for a few minutes over so that Mr. Tracol and I can both address you today since we had incorrectly anticipated that Mr. Kremer would be briefer in his submissions, at least in answering questions. I'll certainly try but may at the end ask for a couple of extra minutes. But I'll let you know at that time, if I don't finish, Mr. President. Thank you. The Prosecution's first ground of appeal, as set out in the appeal brief, is that the Trial Chamber erred in holding that certain crimes committed by Mr. Martinovic did not constitute persecution, though finding that they were -- the crimes were crimes against humanity. There is three specific incidents raised in the Prosecution's brief, ones in relation to the conviction under crimes against humanity pertaining to the beatings of detainees, the second, once again, is for a conviction of crimes against humanity for unlawful labour, that's for inhumane and cruel treatment as a result of the labour of detainees within his area of responsibility, and the third is also unlawful labour but it's the specific incidents of the wooden rifles. The issue before Your Honours if I may characterise it for you is the correctness of the Trial Chamber's approach and the reasonableness of their factual conclusions. It's the Prosecution's submission that the Trial Chamber approached its task incorrectly and made factual conclusions which no reasonable Trial Chamber could make. I will first start by just considering the general factual or circumstantial findings by the Trial Chamber in this regard and in the Prosecution's submission they are compelling. There was a widespread and systematic attack against the Muslim part of the civilian population with the specific aim of transforming the formerly ethnically mixed area in and around Mostar in into a Bosnian Croat territory with an ethnically pure Bosnian Croat population. Secondly, the Trial Chamber found that the acts or for which Mr. Martinovic was convicted comprised part of there widespread and systematic attack and his acts directly contributed to the overall aim of the campaign. The overall aim of the campaign was discriminatory. Trial Chamber found that Mr. Martinovic with the knowledge of the attack decided to pursue the goal of the attack; once again, the goal was discriminatory. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Martinovic carried out the arrest and detention of the civilian population of Mostar on May the 9th and he did it with discriminatory intent against Muslims. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Martinovic carried out forcible transfers from Mostar of civilians and he did it with discriminatory intent against Muslims. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Martinovic participated in the plunder of homes in Mostar, and he did it with discriminatory intent against Muslims. The evidence of the trial is that Mr. Martinovic called detainees who were taken from the Heliodrom for unlawful labour, discriminatory names or derogatory or called them in derogatory terms. Specifically owe called them balijas, which is a derogatory term for Muslims. He called them fundamentalists or extremists. In my submission this clearly exhibits discriminatory intent. Every time detainees were chosen for unlawful labour, they were Muslim. The paragraphs for which the detainees working in the area of Vinko Skrobo Brigade were paragraphs 263 to 273. The paragraphs for the wooden rifles incident, the findings were at 274 to 292, and the beatings were at paragraphs 382 to 389. I have attempted to look at all the victims listed in the footnotes for each one of the findings in relation to the crimes against humanity found by the Trial Chamber, and unless I'm mistaken, each one of the victims referred to in the paragraphs related to the findings of those three incidents were Muslim. Of the victims for which Martinovic is convicted in these three incidents for unlawful labour and beatings, not one is a Bosnian Croat detainee. And despite this powerful and compelling evidence, some of it which I will come back to, the Trial Chamber concluded that for every single incident of unlawful labour and beatings there was no discriminatory basis for the choice of Muslim detainees. The Trial Chamber concluded that it had not been proven in each specific incident that the crimes were carried out on a discriminatory basis. What I'll come back to is the Trial Chamber's approach here, which is that it approached each incident separately. They attempted to identify on a case-by-case basis whether the crimes were carried out with discrimination. I'll come back to the paragraphs but if you look at paragraph 693, which is the wooden rifle incident, the Trial Chamber simply concluded at 693 in the second-last sentence, "However no evidence was introduced regarding the grounds upon which the four prisoners involved were selected." With respect, it will be the Prosecution's submissions and I'll go through paragraph 693 and, more importantly, 692 to indicate that the focus on determining whether or not there was evidence of the basis upon which these four were selected was the wrong approach. This approach of looking simply and solely as to the basis of their selection erred by focusing on the specific incident, and the specific basis on which they were chosen at that specific time. With respect, that's much too narrow. If you look at paragraph 692 of the judgement, the second full sentence states, "The Prosecution has, however, not led evidence sufficient evidence, to prove that the prisoners were taken to perform labour on the basis of their specific religious, political, or racial background." With respect it's almost as if the Trial Chamber's analysis is frozen in time. Limiting itself to asking the question why were these Muslim detainees chosen? The question they should have asked themselves is s there any other reason other than the fact that they were Muslim? There is no reference in these two paragraphs to the context of the attack and there is no reference to the circumstances surrounding the use of Bosnian Muslims in unlawful labour and human shields. My submission's because they focussed on the specific incident. The context is relevant the circumstances are relevant and this Appeals Chamber in the Kovacka appeal judgement at paragraph 366 stated "discriminatory intent may be inferred from the context of the attack, provided that it is substantiated by the surrounding circumstances at the time." What were the factual elements of the context in this case? I've mentioned many of them at the beginning of my submissions but it was the general discriminatory nature of the attack that the attack was only against Muslims, that those detained were Muslims, that those taken out for unlawful labour were Muslims, and that Martinovic, with knowledge of the discriminatory nature of the widespread and systematic attack, decided to pursue the goal. Did any of these find their way into the judgement? In my submission in relation to these paragraphs, no. What are the surrounding circumstances that should have been taken into account. As you're aware in the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber judgement the Court indicated that the surrounding circumstances could substantiate the finding and they looked at the operation of the prison in Krnojelac, the systematic nature of the crimes, and, interestingly, in Krnojelac they looked at the general attitude of the perpetrator. Not whether in this individual case he indicated that they were taken out at that specific date for the specific reason that they were Muslim, but his general attitude as a circumstance. In this case, the surrounding circumstances include that only Muslims were used in the incidents referred to by the Trial Chamber in relation to Mr. Martinovic, the derogatory treatment of Muslims by Mr. Martinovic, and that he acted with discriminatory intent in evicting them and forcibly transferring them and plundering them. It's the Prosecution submission that if you look at the context of the circumstances and the treatment there is no reasonable doubt that it was discriminatory. But let me look at paragraph 692 again with you, if I may, and take you through some of the evidence upon which the Court found that there was -- the Prosecution had not led sufficient evidence to prove that they were taken to perform labour. Paragraph 692 is based on findings regarding the labour of persons in the area of Mr. Martinovic's brigade and that's -- those findings, the factual findings, start at two -- at paragraph 268. If I could just take you to paragraph 268, Your Honours. That's at page 94. The first sentence of paragraph 268 of the judgement indicates that numerous -- "there was numerous testimonies from prisoners who were forced to perform military support tasks in extremely dangerous conditions such as digging trenches near the confrontation line." Footnote 722. Let's look down to paragraph 722. The second witness it mentions says according to witness J the work consisted of filling sandbags and digging trenches. Let's just go to the testimony of Witness J and if I can ask that the testimony of Witness J be pulled up on screen. Is the testimony before you, Your Honours? Is the testimony before you, Your Honours? I'm sorry. It's on screen? Thank you. The Court had referred to Witness J in footnote 722 in support of its conclusion that there was unlawful labour in the digging of trenches near the confrontation line. Witness J's testimony: In relation to that incident, Witness J speaks about when he was picked up and when he went to work for Martinovic. He was picked up by Martinovic's driver at the Heliodrom and was taken to Stela's command or headquarters. He was asked the first part of the passage, which is before you, as the end of a question. "Did you ever hear Stela use any particular terms or language in referring to Muslims?" The answer: "A term? He called us extremists and at times balijas but mostly he referred to us as extremists. "Now in connection with this Stela, just so the record is clear, did you hear the name in reference to this same person Martinovic? "I did, yes. His full name is Vinko Martinovic and his nickname is Stela." The Trial Chamber though, referring to Witness J, for the purpose of finding that he was used for unlawful labour and fortifications in 262 concludes later in 693 that there was no evidence that witness J was treated or was chosen because of his religious or racial or Muslim background. With respect, this demonstrates in my submission that it's clear the way he was treated. Now, whether or not in every instance the Prosecution can demonstrate that each time he was taken out that there were some words said to him from which you could draw the direct inference is a different matter. That's where the Trial Chamber erred. If I can keep at paragraph 268, once again, footnote 722, the next witness referred to in footnote 722 is Witness PP, once again for the purpose of demonstrating the findings that there was unlawful labour. Let's look at Witness PP's testimony. If you go to his testimony in the transcripts at paragraph 6086, Witness PP was asked by the Prosecution about his involvement with Mr. Martinovic, Stela, in relation to the work he had done. If I can just read to you the passage that is before you. "First of all, how do you know that this man was Stela?" Answer: "Because I had seen him before." Question: "And when had you seen him before?" Answer: "I had seen him when coming to work, when he came to verbally abuse us, calling us names, balija, cattle, things like that, when he came to advise us as we were digging or doing some other kind of work. Mostly in the morning when we were brought to work he would show up so I knew his face. I knew that this was Stela." Once again the Trial Chamber though relying on Witness PP for the purpose of finding that there was unlawful labour, apparently looked at the specific incident and not at what the witness said in terms of the circumstances surrounding their labour. If I can take you to footnote 724. Under 724, related to the Trial Chamber's findings regarding fortification labour, it's referred to and relied on Witness OO. Once again if I can just take you to testimony of Witness OO, he talks about when he would arrive, after being taken from the Heliodrom he talks about the time period, and he says that "I remember well when we arrived there. We were 20 to 30 men per group. He would line us up outside his command which was a red building. On such occasions, most of the men would be mistreated by Stela. He would call us extremists, fundamentalists and various other names." I intend to make the same points with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen would like to put you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, if the Accused calls some detainees who are selected to labour, "cattle" or "extremists," does it follow that they were selected for labour because the Accused thought of them as cattle or as extremists?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The point I was trying to make was that the names that were called were reflective of their being Muslims, not that they were the ABiH army which is -- which I will come to, which is the rationale given by the Trial Chamber. And that this showed his -- this language, cattle or whatever other words you want to use, showed his treatment against them in the way he dealt with them, yes, and that extreme -- I'm sorry, you have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a related question. Were there detainees from other nationalities who might have been selected to do labour but who were not selected to do labour?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In the detention centre in the Heliodrom there were also Bosnian Croat detainees and they were not selected. Thank you. In light of the time I won't pull up on screen the passages but I will simply explain to you the remaining passages that I wanted to refer to and it's actually in relation to footnote 734. Once again this is to support a finding by the Trial Chamber for its finding that detainees were forced to work and that they were involuntary, and the transcripts at paragraph 1679 indicates that when he arrived the following words were said to him as he was sitting there after being brought to the Bulevar. This is transcripts 1679. "When he saw us," and the he is Stela, "when he saw us sitting there he immediately resorted to foul language and more or less said stand up balijas, do you know who you have come to work for? And he said his name was Stela." In footnote 736, there is reference to Witness K, and this witness is referred to for the atmosphere that surrounded the persons doing labour along the confrontation lines. I would submit that the atmosphere surrounding the use of detainees for labour on the confrontation lines is exactly the type of contextual, or, actually in this case, circumstance evidence that the court would look at. Witness K testified in private session so I will not point out in public proceedings what the statements were. But if you look at transcripts 1581 to 1582 you'll see that in the passages that I've previously read to you, the same comments are made in the context of the atmosphere for persons conducting labour. A few more points, as I've run out of time, to allow Mr. Tracol to say a few things. Three of the witnesses, Witness H, Witness KK and Witness YY were civilians. In the wooden rifle incident there were four persons who were taken to use for wooden rifles. Three of them testified. Of those three, two of them were HVO members. They were actually Muslim members serving in the HVO who were arrested. So the statement that the Trial Chamber makes in the footnote to paragraph 692 that they were chosen because they were members of the ABiH is not true. One of the witnesses who testified, Witness I, about the wooden rifle incidents also said that he was a Muslim member of the HVO. He had been in the Territorial Defence, was placed under the command of the HVO, had actually fought with the HVO and then was arrested because he was must almost and then sent to the Heliodrom. All of them, all four of the witnesses in relation to the wooden rifle incidents speak of derogatory comments that were made. There is no basis for differentiating what happened to these four victims previously and to what happened to them when they were committing unlawful labour. There is nothing that would cause the cost to have a reasonable doubt as to the discriminatory nature of the use of these detainees. And as the Krnojelac appeals Chamber stated a case by case approach, and in my submission, as in this case, demonstrates that the Trial Chamber was misled, and it was misled by its own approach to the evidence. The passage which is found in paragraph 692, footnote 1685, where the Court says that as a footnote that to support its findings, that there wasn't discriminatory intent, at footnote 1685 says "the Chamber is satisfied that the prisoners were used," this is all the prisoners in relation to the unlawful labour, "were used because Vinko Martinovic would have used the enemy to perform the dangerous tasks rather than their own soldiers," and Witness SS testified that he believed he was selected because he had served in the ABiH army. That may very well be the case and it may very well be the case that in that circumstances if he was selected as a member and targeted on that basis that the Trial Chamber might have had a reasonable doubt. The error is extrapolating from one witness's testimony about one incident that that witness experienced to the findings in relation to every single detainee for whom the Court found that they had committed unlawful labour. The evidence that I put before you today demonstrates, in my submission, respectfully, that the Trial Chamber was clearly wrong. Those are my submissions on the issue of persecution. I see that I'm close to the end of time. I would just ask for a few minutes for Mr. Tracol to address you on cumulative convictions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, you still have three minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. Tracol to be brief but I may ask for a few more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tracol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will now address the fourth ground of appeal of the Prosecution relating to cumulative convictions. This ground of appeal relates to the error committed, an error committed on a point of law by the Trial Chamber by not entering a conviction for Naletilic based on the same facts for torture as a crime against humanity pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute, 5(F) of the Statute, for mistreatment of the witnesses FF and Z, count 9 of the indictment, in addition to a conviction for persecution pursuant to Article 5(H) of the Statute, count 1 of the indictment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The Trial Chamber refused to enter a cumulative conviction for torture on the following legal ground. In paragraph 724 of the judgement, which I shall now quote, "when an accused is found guilty of persecution and another crime against humanity, the conviction that is upheld is that of persecution." The position of the Prosecution run as follows: The Trial Chamber has erred in law whether it applied the cumulative conviction test as it has been construed by the Appeals Chamber in the relevant jurisprudence. The findings of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 720 to 728 of the judgement do not comply with the findings of the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 1040 to 1043 in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement. As the Appeals Chamber concluded in the Kordic and Cerkez -- concluded the discriminatory actor should be proven as well as the act that the act or omission was committed with an intention to discriminate. On the other hand, whereas torture is enough to establish that a fundamental right has been denied or infringed upon, torture is not required to convict an accused for persecution. Persecution therefore contain elements which are materially distinct from torture. In addition, torture requires proof of the fact that there has been infliction by an act or an omission of pain or acute suffering, both physical and mental, the material element; and on the other hand, proof of a specific intent, namely with a view to obtaining information or confession to punish, intimidate, or force a victim or third party or to discriminate for whatever reason. This concerns mens rea as regards the definition of torture. I refer to the Kunarac judgement paragraph 142 to 144. Proof of these two elements is not required for persecution. Torture, therefore, requires proof of two materially distinct elements from persecution. The Prosecution submits that if it applies the same rationale, the grounds in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement would logically give rise to the finding of the Appeals Chamber that cumulative conviction for persecution and torture is legitimate in that it relies on the same facts pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. The appropriate -- if cumulative conviction were to be applied in the correct manner, the Appeals Chamber should enter a conviction for persecution on the one hand, according to 5(H) of the Statute, in 5(F), torture as crimes which would be legally distinct. This complies with the Kordic and Cerkez judgement. In the interests of justice it would not cause Naletilic to be justifiably prejudiced. That's why I have finished and concluded, Your Honours. The Prosecution requires from the Appeals Chamber that you enter a conviction for torture as a crime against humanity, count 9 of the indictment, in addition to the conviction entered by the Trial Chamber -- by the Trial Chamber for persecution in that it relies on the same facts for persecution pursuant to Article 5(H) of the Statute, count 1 of the indictment. I'm prepared to answer any of your questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are no questions from the Bench, Mr. Tracol, so this ends the submission of the Prosecutor. [English] We will have a response by counsel for Naletilic, we have now 30 minutes and then after the break another 30 minutes for its submission. So, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As to the Prosecution's ground on persecution, that does not apply to Mr. Naletilic. Of course I'll have no remarks about that. The second ground of appeal of the Prosecution as to unlawful labour has been withdrawn. Of course I have no response; no response is needed to that. As to the deportation issue, Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic stand in the same position on that point of law, so for purposes of expediency, if you like, the Naletilic Defence will rely on the submissions to be made by Mr. Kerns on that issue. So all I have to speak about now is the issue of the cumulative conviction which is now sought by the Prosecution. As I understand their argument, what they desire now is a conviction for persecution predicated on torture for which there has already been a conviction. I respectfully submit that this issue has been virtually identically dealt with in the Krstic appeal case and four of this Chamber were on that particular Appeal Chamber as well, and in that case, the Prosecution sought in a similar fashion, multiple convictions; that is, they sought a conviction, they -- at the trial level recognition achieved a conviction for persecution based on murder and yet on appeal asked not only that -- they not only wanted to obviously uphold that conviction for persecution, they also wanted a murder conviction upon which that persecution conviction was predicated. The Chamber disallowed that point and found that such a cumulative conviction as sought in the Krstic appeal case would be improper under the established law of the Tribunal, and the Appeals Chamber relied on a case that I am familiar with the Blockburger case from the United States Supreme Court. And pardon me if I sound pedantic here just briefly. The Blockburger test as -- as -- is essentially set out and in the Prosecution's brief also referred to as the Celebici test, which says that multiple convictions entered under different statutory provisions but based on the same conduct are permissible only if each statutory provision involved has a material -- materially distinct element not contained in the other. I try to think simply when it comes to these things and what that means is this: Is that a -- you have two offences, let's say, one that has the elements, A, B, and C. You have another offence which has the elements of A, B, C, and D. The Blockburger test tells us that convictions for both of those offences based upon the same conduct cannot stand. The offences must -- in order to support cumulative convictions each of them must have an element that the other does not. For example, if one offence has the elements A, B, C, and another offence has the elements A, B, D, fine, the convictions, multiple convictions may stand. What we have presented to us today by the Prosecution is the former not the latter circumstance, that that is that they are seeking now a conviction for what would be characterised as a lesser included offence. A lesser included offence under the doctrine of Blockburger. They seek a conviction for torture which is necessarily already included in the Trial Chamber's conviction of Mr. Naletilic for persecution. As such cumulative convictions in this instance are not warranted and, I suggest, not permissible under the law of this Tribunal. Thank you. May I have one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask you a question in this context, Mr. Hennessy? Are you referring in making your point to the Blockburger test? Are you referring to the Blockburger test, let me start with that. You referred it as concerning the statutory provisions. Now, are you dealing now with the statutory provisions or with the concrete situation found by the Trial Chamber? Can you clarify me about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: I'll try if I understand your question. That necessarily the Blockburger test, it begins and centres on the facts, of course, because we don't have a situation where Blockburger concerns are triggered at all unless we are seeking to punish twice for the same conduct. So the facts -- what we are talking about -- if we are talking about the same set of facts, multiple convictions cannot be obtained unless the two offences in question each have a different element. Now, if you're asking -- if, well, let's say beyond the Statute under practical concerns, if even practically speaking the elements are the same, Blockburger is still triggered. I'll speak concretely now as to what the Prosecution seeks. What the Prosecution is seeking is a cumulative conviction, a second conviction, for conduct which they have already obtained a conviction for, and that conviction is necessarily predicated, that is the persecution conviction, is necessarily predicated on the additional conviction which they now seek. As with my example with the elements being A, B, C or A, B, C, D, it is the former situation. They are seeking a conviction for a lesser included offence of persecution under these particular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you are challenging the definition of the crimes or are you challenging the -- remain with my question. Are you challenging the definition of the crimes of torture and persecution in the sense they would not have different elements except your definition, your example of A, B, C or A, B, D, so you are maintaining that torture would have elements AB, say, and persecution would have A, B, C, but you don't find a different shading element in torture? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: I am, Judge, Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But I didn't see you -- I didn't hear you argue that exactly. Would you be more -- give your arguments on that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Well, and I get back to -- my fact-based argument here is that what the Prosecution is seeking is a second conviction for conduct they have already obtained a conviction for. That being persecution. And as I understand the Prosecution's argument, that even though a conviction for persecution has been obtained based on torture, they now want a separate conviction based on that same torture. That is how Blockburger is triggered, that is how the appeal judgement in Krstic is triggered and in my submission, both of those authorities dictate that a cumulative conviction is not permissible in this circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hennessy, may I ask you one question, which is like this: Is it conceivable that there could be torture without persecution? That's possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Absolutely. And if I may, to continue along that, what we have here and what I understand the Prosecution to be seeking is now that they have obtained a conviction predicated on torture committed under discriminatory grounds, on a discriminatory basis, that being persecution, they now also want the lesser included offence of torture. Again, I say that that's impermissible pursuant to the Krstic appeal judgement. Are there any more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You did invite any other questions, so let me ask you this. Would you say that persecutions as a crime is directed to different element of torture? To build on what you just accepted, there can be torture without persecutions. Are the two crimes directed to different factual elements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: The answer is both yes and no, and let me expand on that. That -- I think it's fair to say that every act of torture is discriminatory in some respect. But the Statute of the Tribunal elevates torture from torture to being a crime of persecution if the discriminatory basis is for certain particular reasons, racial, political, and otherwise. So while, yes, I can't practically speaking every torture must necessarily involve some discriminatory process, but only certain types of that -- only certain times of discrimination elevate torture to persecution. May I have a moment to consult with my co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sure, you may consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: That concludes our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, then I understand you don't need the half an hour at the beginning of the afternoon for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Not unless you want me to keep talking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. So we can take our break now and we'll reconvene at 2.30. 2.30 for the response by Martinovic. The meeting is adjourned. --- Break taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody, and we will now continue with the response by Martinovic. So I'll give the floor to counsel for Martinovic for their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: May it please this honourable court and may it please my friends of the Prosecution counsel. Your Honours, as you have heard my name is Kurt Kerns and I have the privilege of responding to the Prosecution's accusations and their appeal this afternoon. We will argue in opposition to the Prosecution's various issues that they've raised. Although the Prosecution originally raised four issues in their appeal I'll only be discussing the first issue and the third issue because, again, two has been withdrawn and four has nothing to do with Mr. Martinovic. The first ground establishes that the Prosecution basically seeks to create a judicially created presumption for which there is no legal authority. Although Mr. Martinovic was convicted of persecution, the persecution claims that the Trial Chamber erred by not inferring discriminatory intent on to three specific instances of wrongful conduct that they allege. I've listened to my learned friend of the Prosecution submit to this Court how the Krnojelac appeals judgement supports his position because in that case the Appeals Chamber did find that there was an error of fact in the finding of discriminatory intent. My submission is that a close and a full reading of the Krnojelac appeal judgement in actuality supports the Defence's position in this case. Why? Because right in paragraph 184 of the Krnojelac judgement, that court specifically held that discriminatory intent cannot be inferred from as applying to a specific wrongful act just by the general discriminatory nature of an attack. In fact, the appellate Chamber said in that case that discriminatory intent can be inferred from such a context under conditions. The specific wording is "as long as circumstances exist surrounding this wrongful act that substantiate authenticate that inference, that general inference." There have to be facts that substantiate the general inference. In other words, you just can't infer discriminatory intent from a general discriminatory nature of an attack. There must be specific facts surrounding the specific incident that substantiate, back up, if you will, that inference. Now, in the Krnojelac case there were facts that substantiated that inference and that's what the Court found. In this case, that evidence is completely lacking and I'll speak in my submissions why that evidence is completely lacking. A full review of the underlying facts in Vinko Martinovic's case substantiate in fact a complete lack of discriminatory intent in how these prisoners were brought to the front line and how these prisoners were brought to his headquarters. The -- all three of these instances for which the Prosecution complains, while they may be described as rude or belligerent or inappropriate or unnecessarily violent, what they cannot be described as is discriminatory against the Muslims based upon religious, political or racial grounds. I'd like to focus on the three instance which the Prosecution focuses on, specifically in paragraph 2.2 of the Prosecution's brief. They are described by the Prosecution as, first, beatings of the detainees at headquarters; secondly, wrongful labour; and thirdly, wooden rifle incident or wooden rifle incidents, depending on who you listen to, but at least here we are dealing with just one wooden rifle incident. Paragraph 382 through 389 of the trial judgement discuss the underlying facts of this first case for which the Prosecution complains. At paragraph 677 of the trial court judgement, that trial court correctly found that no beatings at the headquarters were carried out on discriminatory grounds. In fact, they concluded exactly the opposite, that these beatings were random, quote, "Without religious, political or racial background." And that was the word that they used, no background to support those facts. The Prosecution in its appeal completely ignores two very important key considerations for this Court to decide. The first, how were these detainees chosen, if at all, by Vinko Martinovic? Secondly, is there evidence in the record of non-discriminatory motives as to these three incidents? Let me address just the evidence that the Trial Chamber felt was important enough to note in their own written judgement. Paragraph 265 of the trial judgement discusses how the Chamber found that detainees were taken from the Heliodrom to Vinko Martinovic. It was alleged that a man named Dinko Knezovic would go to the Heliodrom, pick up detainees and the extent of the order that the Trial Chamber said came from Vinko was go get X number of men. Not go get ten Muslims, just go get ten men. It needs to be recalled that the Heliodrom was originally a military prison. The Heliodrom, it must be understood, is not comparable to the KP Dom detention facility in the Krnojelac case where Serbs in the Krnojelac case were separated from non-Serbs and only non-Serbs were being discriminated against as a matter of policy. We don't have that situation here. Initially, there is no evidence before the Trial Chamber or before this Court to suggest that Vinko Martinovic had any say in how the Heliodrom, number 1, housed prisoners, or secondly how the Heliodrom sent prisoners his way, unlike the accused in Krnojelac where he was actually working at the detention centre. There is evidence that HVO prisoners and Muslim prisoners were held in the same section of the Heliodrom as well, unlike in the Krnojelac case. Transcript 6541. There was no policy at the Heliodrom to only mistreat Muslim prisoners unlike the KP Dom and the Krnojelac case and secondly there was no evidence to suggest that Vinko, number 1, knew anything about it and, number 2, had any say in the matter. While it is true that the majority of the detainees in the Heliodrom were in fact Muslims, it is also true that the majority of the forces in the ABiH were Muslim. So when Vinko allegedly says bring me ten men or 20 men or 30 men, how can one say that they are being targeted based upon racial, religious, or political views? As I mentioned the Prosecution also ignores completely in its submissions actual evidence of non-discriminatory intent, and asks this court to impose on appeal discriminatory motives, in spite of actual evidence of non-discriminatory motives. Let me show you some examples. In the beating incident for which the Prosecution complains, one of the detainees was found hit and the explanation is found in paragraph 387 of the trial judgement. It says he was beat because he had been found hiding. That was the motive. Another was alleged that a man was punched and a witness testified that this man was punched and hit because he had made a comment about my client's father and he refused to let go of a bag when he was getting on a bus. This is referred to as this Professor incident found at paragraph 386 of the trial judgement, specifically footnote 1010. There is specific proof in these incidents that they were not done with discriminatory intent. Now, while these facts, if proved, may have constituted cruel treatment, the crime of persecution has a mandatory element, an additional element that must be proved, not just proved but proved beyond and to the exclusion of all reasonable doubt and that is this discriminatory intent. One cannot meet that burden here today on appeal through a general overall inference of discrimination. I want to mention the language of the Krnojelac appeal again because again it supports my client's position. At paragraph 184, the appellate Chamber said that in determining the existence of discriminatory intent the Trial Chamber can consider, and I quote, "The general attitude of the perpetrator." What did the Trial Chamber know about Vinko Martinovic's general attitude? It was cited in the judgement. It was even cited specifically in their summary. He was brought up in an ethnically diverse area of Mostar called Rodoc with friends that he worked in close association with that were Muslims. He worked in close association with Muslims, the Court found. He lived in close association with Muslims. When the conflict in Mostar began against the Serb and Montenegrin army, he fought alongside the Muslims as comrades in arms. A quote from the Trial Chamber, "He was never engaged politically." He was a local Mostar boy with a basic education, found specifically at paragraph 37 of the trial court's summary judgement. In Krnojelac the Appeals Chamber in the very last sentence of paragraph 184 holds that in discerning discriminatory intent a fact finder can consider, and I quote, "the general attitude of the perpetrator." If you just plug in a word search into this huge 20.000-page transcript, general attitude, what you're going to find when it relates to Vinko Martinovic is that several witnesses are popped up saying, "His general attitude was that he treated BH Muslims and BH Croats the same." The words from Krnojelac and the words from the trial court and the words from the witness all match as to his general attitude. His general attitude was the same towards BH Muslims and BH Croats. Trial judgement 757 confirmed -- at paragraph 757 confirmed witnesses testifying to that effect. Therefore, while the Trial Chamber did go on to say, Well, but Vinko wasn't as nice as he should have been to most Muslims, and he should have been more helpful to others, there is substantial evidence in this record and in the facts of this case for the fact finder to rule and say to the Prosecution, Prosecution, we are not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt as to these three acts for which you complain because you did not establish that in those three acts there was discriminatory intent. Other facts that substantiate a lack of intent are found at paragraph 384 of the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber "accepts that Vinko helped and protected some Muslim prisoners." Footnote 1.000 lists a series of witnesses who spoke about how Vinko Martinovic protected them and helped them, his Muslim neighbours. He hid them from forces in his basement. He paid them and when one was injured he actually took him to the hospital very quickly. It was the testimony of these Muslim witnesses on Vinko's behalf. Footnote 1.718 discusses how many Muslims wanted to go to the -- wanted to go to Vinko Skrobo's unit because they felt protected and safe there versus anywhere else. These were Muslim witnesses testifying to that effect. The point being that the Trial Chamber had ample evidence to support its decision that proof of discriminatory motive was lacking. The Krnojelac decision is supportive. Why? Because that Chamber held that the court could consider the overall evidence to determine if there is discriminatory intent. The other two incidents that the Prosecution asks this Court to essentially convict by inference involve wrongful labour, referred to in paragraph 692, and this wooden rifle incident referred to in paragraph 693 of the trial judgement. The Prosecution seems to focus on the wooden rifle incident a little bit more so let me address that. Again, how were these detainees selected according to the Trial Chamber's findings? A man named Dinko Knezovic goes to the Heliodrom and asks for 30 prisoners. Not 30 Muslim prisoners, just 30 prisoners. Just 30 people. Mr. Knezovic then, according to the facts the Trial Chamber relied on, took these 30 to the headquarters of the Vinko Skrobo ATG. What was the Prosecutor's evidence of Vinko Martinovic's involvement in their selection? The trial court noted it at paragraph 276, at the top of page 98 of the trial judgement and you have it. Vinko Martinovic then ordered Ernest Tadic to select four people of those 30. That's it. So what you have is a man named -- I'm going to miss pronounce his name, Dinko, going over to the Heliodrom bringing back some people and then Vinko says to a guy named Ernest, "Ernest, pick four." Now, tell me how that is done on the basis of discriminatory intent? Even if all of the facts that you hear in this trial judgement are considered true, which we don't concede. All that was alleged was that Vinko said out of 30 prisoners, "Ernest, get four of them." There is absolutely zero evidence that these men were targeted with specific discriminatory intent. The Trial Chamber found very specifically that while this wooden rifle incident constituted unlawful labour, in fact convicted of that, they did not find an additional crime of persecution. Why? Because no evidence was adduced. In fact, there was a tide of evidence to the contrary, which they could not just put out of their mind. Now, my learned friend the Prosecutor argues, well, let's just infer it. Let's just assume it. Because there was an overall discrimination and because he used words like balija and extremist on a few occasions. After all, the argument goes, Muslims were discriminated generally and victimised generally, and in fact they argue Vinko was even convicted of persecution as it related to these unlawful transfers. So the argument of the Prosecution goes that when Vinko says "Dinko bring me 30 men and Ernest pick four of them," what he really meant to say was, "But make sure they are Muslims because I have the intent to discriminate," which does not make sense and I submit that to this honourable court those submissions must fail. Why were these detainees used? The Trial Chamber again made specific findings of fact and you'll recall that one of the very first things we heard when we came in here yesterday morning was that the Trial Chamber doesn't evaluate the entire facts de novo, they are afforded deference. What were the Trial Chamber's factual findings? Footnote 1685, Your Honours, is very key to this issue because it flat out says that the Chamber is satisfied. Note the word satisfied. That means they are convinced that the prisoners were used because Vinko Martinovic would have rather used the enemy soldiers than his own soldiers to commit dangerous tasks. They were satisfied on the facts that that was the motive, that that was the reason. Yet the Prosecution submits that in spite of the satisfaction, in spite of being convinced of this, that there is a huge miscarriage of justice here. Again, at paragraph 694 of the trial judgement the Court found no evidence has been adduced that these prisoners were selected on the basis of their religious or political views. The entirety of the facts, all of the facts that came out in trial, satisfied them that that was not done for that reason. Your Honours, every war in the history of man kind has, as at its core, some element of discrimination. But not every bad act within a war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. constitutes a crime of persecution. In fact, this rather obvious truth was specifically found by the Court -- by the appellate Chamber in the Krnojelac case where the appellate Chamber held that discriminatory intent cannot be inferred simply by looking at the overall discriminatory nature. In fact footnote 267 in Krnojelac flat out says that not every attack against the civilian population is necessarily discriminatory. Your Honours, there was no evidence in this wooden rifle incident or in the wrongful labour incidents that these detainees were selected for any other reason than they were prisoners of war. The Trial Chamber made that factual conclusion based upon a review of all of the evidence, and at paragraph 677 and 692 they made specific factual determinations. In fact, the Trial Chamber pointed out in footnote 1.685 that Witness SS said he was chosen because he was in the opposing army. And yet the Prosecution complains, well, that was with discriminatory intent. It needs to be stressed that Mr. Stringer's efforts, he's the Prosecutor that actually wrote the appeal my learned friend has to argue today, but in his appeal there is also another glaring problem and that is that in the appellate brief they argue for de novo review before there Chamber on this issue. And as we as Defence lawyers and prosecutors are also often reminded the Trial Chamber's factual findings are afforded and accorded deference and are not to be disturbed unless they are clearly arbitrary. Here, we do not have anything close to clearly arbitrary findings when you consider the totality of the circumstances and the totality of the evidence in relation to these three instances that are complained of. The Trial Chamber's specific findings as to my client's specific intent were based on consideration, review, testimony, and exhibits. And my argument is that one can no sooner make an apple into an orange by calling it an orange than one can make legal issues out of factual issues by calling them legal issues. Which is exactly what the Prosecution is doing in their appellate brief. The assertion that the Trial Chamber incorrectly applied the law is nothing more than a thinly veiled attempt to manufacture legal issues out of a factual determination. And Your Honours, as to this issue of persecution and whether or not no reasonable fact finder could have a doubt, I submit that the Trial Chamber was correct when it found at bare minimum we've got a doubt as to this discriminatory intent. It is simply on the other hand manifestly unjust to come before an appellate Chamber and argue that these three instances should have discriminatory intent imposed upon them in the face of the tide of evidence to the contrary. Or, worse yet, to say no reasonable person could make and have a reasonable doubt. One of the most glaring defects with the Prosecution's argument is found at paragraph 211, subparagraph 4, and my learned colleague even referred to that same argument today in his oral submissions. Here the Prosecution submits this: That unless an accused comes forward with specific evidence that the crime was committed on some other specific ground, the Court must find discriminatory intent. Now, recognise the logic of that submission. In its effect they are saying assume this exists, once general predicate facts are established. Assume discrimination exists for everything. Then place the burden -- yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm lost a little. It might be my own fault. I can't find paragraph 211 subparagraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Page 12 of the Prosecution's appeal brief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Oh, the Prosecution's appeal brief. I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I can get that to the Court, if you like. I've got a copy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. My question serves two purposes, first to keep the record straight and give you the possibility to answer the question, if you so want. You referred us at page 68 -- 68, line 4 and 5 to paragraph 384, and there it reads, the Trial Chamber "accepts that Vinko helped and protected some Muslim prisoners." But my reading of this paragraph is, "the Chamber accepts that Vinko Martinovic may have helped and protected some of BH Muslim prisoners with whom he or his family had a personal relationship or others who may have bought his protection. However, reliable and corroborated evidence submitted by a number of Prosecution witnesses shows that this protection was only granted to a handful of Muslims." This would be the quote in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, and I would also refer the Court, though, in that same paragraph, I believe it's that same paragraph -- no, the following paragraph, to footnote 1.000 where the Trial Chamber then goes on to list all of the -- well, at least many of the witnesses that testified as to my client's assistance. In other words, our submission is that while they may have made that ruling as stated in paragraph 384, they also understood that many of these people testified that he was helping them and those factual determinations as stated in these footnotes are certainly relevant in determining whether you have a reasonable doubt, if I've answered the Court's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, you have provided us with a detailed description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start again. You gave us a detailed description to high light in a number of cases the fact that your client had no discriminatory intent. However, you did not talk about the labour of the detainees, whether forced labour or not. Whether they worked and did this job willingly, you didn't establish a connection between that and a discriminatory intent. I would like you to elaborate this, please, and, if possible, if you could give us some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As to whether or not -- the answer is mixed. I believe the testimony at trial was some volunteered and wanted to come to Vinko's unit to work and others did not. In fact there was a conviction entered by the trial court as to unlawful labour. So there isn't a clear response either way as to whether or not they were all volunteers or they were all forced because the evidence was conflicting. Many were volunteers, others, the Prosecution alleged, were forced to conduct this type of behaviour. In any event, the Prosecution complains of simply three small incidents, one -- and that they are referred to in paragraph 2.2. One was the beatings at the Bulevar, at the front line; the second, the unlawful labour at the front line; and then third, this wooden rifle incident. And in their appeal they limited the scope of what they were appealing to those three issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What kind of tasks were -- what kind of job did they have to do? Or what did they have to do? Those who were willing to work, what kind of jobs were they doing? Did they -- were they of a military nature or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Some, and again I wasn't the lawyer through trial so I'm only left with what -- my colleague is -- he was trial counsel but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Your Honours, since this concerns factual issues, I would propose to give you an answer in several sentences. So if the question was what did these prisoners do, the prisoners came, and we saw how they came, to the headquarters. Their task was to perform light jobs and certain manual artisan-type jobs at the front line, in order to make it perfectly clear, can we please put on the ELMO P14.5? This is a photograph depicting the front line and it will become instantly clear to you what jobs it was possible to perform at this location. Therefore, if all of you can see this on your screens, this is a demarcation line between the two sides. This street is called Bulevar. Bulevar separates Mostar into two parts, the western Mostar and the eastern part. Croatian units are here in this section closest to us and on the other side, where you see a lot of devastation, this is where the positions of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were. The red portion marks the area held by the unit of Vinko Martinovic, and next to it is the so-called health care centre. At that point in time, at the health care centre, it was the soldiers who were positioned there. 20 metres further there were soldiers of the opposing side. Nobody came to work there because there was nothing to dig there. One cannot dig in the asphalt, not a fly could fly through this area. That's how close these sides were to each other. I did not earlier present our objections to all the testimony we heard about filling sandbags, digging, and so on. There was nothing to dig here. No trenches were dug there because people were shooting from the buildings. So what is it that the prisoners did? The prisoners were not here on this location. No, they were at the headquarters which is one block further away and protected, away from this front line. So what is it they came -- that they went to do there? They went there to make some repairs, some of them came here and said I made coffee or I repaired cars and so on. So they did the ongoing tasks, whatever was needed. This is what they did. They did not go to the front line. I will now yield the floor to my colleague once again. These are the factual clarifications. Thank you for allowing me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honours, I was stating that one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kerns, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for correcting my error and drawing my attention to the Prosecution's appeals brief which I've now consulted on the relevant point. In paragraph 211, it appears to me that the Prosecution was not relying merely on these beatings, et cetera, but was relying on something else. Paragraph opens this way, "The Prosecution submits that, 1, where there is a widespread or systematic attack that has a discriminatory aim, such that the victims are targeted on relevant discriminatory grounds (in this case an attack against BH Muslims with the aim of transforming the area in the territory populated by an ethnically pure BH Croat population), then, 2, where a person accused of persecution is a participant in that widespread or systematic attack and commits relevant crime during the course of that widespread or systematic attack," then comes 3 and 4, and in the conclusion is that the only reasonable conclusion is, so, one of persecution. And there was the necessary discriminatory intent. So is seems to me from that paragraph the Prosecution, while casting its net very widely, including all factors and all circumstances, wasn't particularly relying on the fact of the beatings and of the wooden rifles, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may I was arguing with regard to their proposed change in the law and if the Court were to continue on after the comma, after the word "attack" that you just mentioned, the words exist, "unless there is some specific evidence that indicates the crime was committed on some other specific ground." And I argue that that is a shifting of the burden of proof. When they say, Hey, let's assume it, unless they can produce some facts to dispute it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I just want to understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: My point was that that would be -- may it please the Court, my point was that to adopt such a suggestion to infer general intent and then place a burden on an accused to prove otherwise would create a shifting of the presumption of innocence as formulated in Article 21(3). Now, I do note in the Prosecution's reply they argue that there would be no impact on the presumption of innocence in their reply brief. They say that the law does allow for permissive inferences and the law does allow for presumptions and of course we agree with that. But what the Prosecution is seeking in this appeal before your honourable judges is not a permissive inference and they are not asking for a rebuttable presumption. What they are asking nor is a mandatory inference that says once general discriminatory intent is established everything bad that ever happens somehow becomes discriminatory in nature. Unless the Defence comes forward and proves otherwise. Placing the burden of proof on the Defence. My point being that the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber's decision is not the prosecutorial saviour that they submit to you that it is, the specific holding states that discriminatory intent may be inferred. That is permissive. It's not mandatory language. As long as there are facts that substantiate that general intent. That is at most a permissive rule of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kerns, is there anything in the judgement which says that the Trial Chamber, in coming to this conclusion of non-discrimination, took into account the point made by the Prosecution that the very attack against the civilian population was based on discriminatory grounds and that the accused participated in that attack? Is there something in the judgement which says that the Trial Chamber adverted to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KERNS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. When you -- in fact, it must be said that the Trial Chamber recognised discriminatory intent when they found it. I refer you to paragraph 680 where they found -- I'll wait. And 681 and 679, all of those paragraphs. Where in all three of those paragraphs, the Trial Chamber is making findings of discriminatory intent. They are saying under the facts here, we find that there was discriminatory intent. Now, they are not shy about finding it when it exists, in fact in one count they convicted my client of persecution based upon discriminatory intent when he -- it was alleged that he assisted in some unlawful transfer. So this isn't a situation where the Prosecution -- I'm sorry, the Trial Chamber is trying to shy away from finding discriminatory intent when the facts suggest to do so. My argument is simply that it should not be imputed to every single bad act that the Prosecution alleges. And I hope I've made myself clear on that point. Pursuant to the scheduling order, I know that I need to address another issue as well with the time that I have, but when my learned colleague stands and suggests to you that no reasonable fact finder could rule as a Trial Chamber did as to these three incidents I would ask the Court to consider the evidence that the Trial Chamber mentioned, which is, among other things, that my client was raised with Muslims, that he had Muslim friends. Even if they were limited, he had them. As my learned colleague, Mr. Par, indicated, an if you're going to convict me for not helping some I should get credit for the ones that I did help. In addition to that they were comrades in war. Muslims testified that he protected them, hid them, his general attitude was the same, that many wanted to go from the Heliodrom to be with him, that he ate them, fed them, in fact that he ate at the same table even during the war. All of those facts are sufficient at bare minimum to cause a reasonable doubt as to these particular incidents, at a bare minimum. My learned friend in his next 30 minutes will have to stand before you when I am done and argue with a straight face that all of these facts that the Trial Chamber heard should somehow be pushed from the mind of the Trial Chamber, ignored completely, and quashed with this huge presumption of discriminatory intent from the general nature. And I would respectfully submit that that is wrong and it should not be done and would result in a switching of the burden of proof. Now, the first issue raised by the Prosecution is the only issue which they ask, albeit kind of halfheartedly but at least they do ask for -- I think they described it as a non-significant increase in my client's sentence. Because that one little paragraph is in their appeal brief, although I do note my learned friend didn't argue such a thing today, I feel compelled to respond to that issue as well because it's a big one to us. Our position on this is that Vinko Martinovic has already received way too much time and a non-significant increase that is suggested only in a one sentence in the Prosecution's brief should be seen for what it is. When the Court makes certain considerations I would ask that the Court consider the findings, that this man was "a Mostar boy with no political connections, with a basic education, responsible for a couple-hundred-metre line that's reflected in the exhibits that we brought before this honourable Chamber. He was not politically connected so we would ask that the Chamber not lose sight of the man Vinko that we are dealing with who was born and raised in Mostar. He did not go out looking for this war. The war came to the streets of his youth and came to him. And he stayed there. There is a very important exhibit in the trial, PP608, where he's even offered promotion. He's even told, Vinko, you can have more power, more prestige, and he refuses it so that he can stay along the front lines with his men. So we are not talking about some huge, powerful commander. We are talking about, as the Trial Chamber found, a Mostar boy defending a couple hundred metres in front of the Exhibit PP. That's what we are dealing with here and that's the man that received 18 years. The same amount of time it takes in America to become a man, 18 years. He's certainly, we believe, would split to this Court, we are not trying to tell you he was a saint, we are not trying to say he was some perfect saint. He certainly was not. But I did not know the 29 year old man that began the fighting in Mostar. I do know the 42 year old man that sits before you and has his fate in your hands today and I stand here proud to call him my friend. A modest yet undefined increase of sentence that the Prosecution halfheartedly suggest in their appeal must fail. Your Honours, I promised I would talk about this deportation issue. So if it please the Court, let me turn to that. Although this third issue raised by the Prosecution seeks no modification as to my client's sentence, the Court in its scheduling order requests that we discuss this issue so if it please I'll turn to that issue. And once again the Prosecution argues the Krnojelac opinion as it's somehow assisting the Prosecution, well, I will argue it does not. At paragraph 4.6 of the Prosecution's response brief, the Prosecution alleges in paragraphs 25 and 26 of the indictment, that it alleges my client committed the crime of deportation. Now, the paragraphs mentioned and quoted by the Prosecution in their response brief at paragraph 4.6, they make no mention of deportation at all. In fact, when you take a look at our indictment, you won't even find the word deportation. It's not there. At almost every time in the indictment, when the indictment refers to forced displacements of people, the indictment talks about forcible transfers, not only is the word deportation not found in the paragraphs the Prosecution says it's found in, the word is not found anywhere in the indictment. The only part of the indictment with any modification of the word deportation is found buried in the 34th paragraph when they are talking about underlying acts and then all that is said in a single sentence is: "Certain men were forcibly transferring and deporting people." All other 16 times that the indictment refers to deported -- or, I'm sorry, to displacing people you find the word forcible transfer. In fact, count 18 charges him with forcible transfer, displacements of people. It should also be noted that the Prosecution's argument on deportation, while interesting, is also irrelevant in the context of this particular case. Because the same underlying conduct for which they complain was covered in the count of persecution based upon unlawful transfer, or forcible transfer as it was called in the indictment. So the Defence's position is that this Trial Chamber could not have found deportation as an additional basis for persecution even if it wanted to. Why? Because it's not even charged in the indictment. The good news is -- even though the bad news is we are charged with some things we didn't know we were charged with, the good news is we were acquitted of things we were not even charged with as well. We are not charged with deportation, but yet there is a comment in the Trial Chamber about how they didn't prove it. Firstly, deportation is not even charged. Yet, the Trial Chamber acquitted us of it which we thank them for, I suppose, but firstly, our position is deportation is not even relevant to this case. Secondly, Vinko's conviction of persecution by means of forcible transfer covered the entirety of these displacements that they alleged. It's even mentioned specifically in count 18 for the forcible transfer. What the Krnojelac appellate Chamber made clear is regardless where people are forcibly displaced the crime of persecution can be established. We agree. We think it's a fine aspect of law. But in our case, displacements that were alleged were from west side to east side of town. And, importantly, the Krnojelac appeal Chamber cited - with approval, I mind you - this very trial judgement, findings of fact at footnote 354 and says, well, they were able to find that forcible transfer constituted the crime of persecution. So this very case was cited with approval. As I said, the deportation issue raised by the Prosecution is in fact irrelevant in the context of this case. Also, in Krnojelac, the appellate Chamber said it is not necessary to define a term which does not appear in the provision upon which the indictment is based. But, on the other hand, I actually bothered to read the whole case and as Judge Schomburg essentially pointed out in Krnojelac, if an appeal Chamber can help define the law it ought to do so. And we agree with that as well. Which makes perfect sense to me. So frankly, our position is we would like to have some part in the development of that jurisprudence as well, so let me address the Defence's position as to deportation recognising our position is it's kind of irrelevant in the context of our case. If this Chamber finds that throwing in a sing the word, deporting, right after the word forcibly transferring in a single sentence in a 58-paragraph, 22-page indictment is sufficient to raise the issue of deportation, as separately charged and defined as a war crime, then our Defence would be as follows: Forcible transfer should be defined as different than deportation. Deportation, we believe, is also a more serious crime than forcible transfer under some circumstances, and deportation should require displacement beyond a de jure border while forcible transfer should be defined as something that takes place within the borders of the state.
