We agree that any form of displacement can be the basis of a persecution crime, but I submit that if one forces a family from the west side of town to the east side of town, then the citizens displaced are still able to speak the language, they may share the same currency, they may have family support or economic support. Conversely, when one displaces a citizen from one country to another where they may not be able to speak the same language, they maybe have no connections, they may have no family, they may not have any of the right currency, that should be treated differently. Because there is an increased amount of damage, harm, and inconvenience. Deportation, we submit, is that crime. I think it also important to note that I heard my learned colleague come up with an impressive article about how so many people have refused to define deportation the way I suggest. I think it's also important to know that just October 6, the same Prosecutor's office is telling the Stakic appeal Chamber exactly the opposite, that they've covered the various jurisprudent sources from the Trial Chambers and we acknowledge that the jurisprudence that is developed is not favourable to our position. I think Judge Guney even asked the question I'm sorry on the third day of the hearing October 6, line 13, "Mr. Tracol you said that after conducting research with the case law of the Tribunal you came to the conclusion that this was not in favour or that this was contrary to the main position of the Prosecution." And again Mr. Tracol goes on to say it's true that when you look at the decision the way the jurisprudence has developed it's not in the main favour of the Prosecution. An interesting question from Judge Guney again: "Regarding the outcome let me ask then on what basis do you maintain this position?" And their answer at the time was the Krnojelac appeal judgement, which failed even to define the issue. Your Honours, my reply to the Prosecutor is done. But when I listened to my learned colleague argue twice in the course of his submission that no reasonable finder of fact could find as the Trial Chamber did as to these three instances, an image popped into my mind of a toy my daughter has, and I mean no disrespect to Norm because I like him very much as a man. Only for illustrative purposes am I saying this. But it reminds me of this figurine my daughter has where the monkeys have their hands over their eyes and their ears and their mouth. Hear no evil, speak no evil, see no evil. Here they are wanting to see evil, speak evil, hear evil without any evidence, or, in the face of a whole lot of evidence that could at least say to the trier of fact, I've got a doubt. And I would submit that that is wrong. I would request that the trial court affirm the Trial Chamber's findings as to these three incidents, affirm that the Court -- the Prosecutor failed to establish beyond and to the exclusion of all doubt because there is a plethora of doubt under the facts that the Trial Chamber discussed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Kerns. I will now turn to the Prosecution for their reply. You have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours. My learned colleagues. I'll only take a few minutes but just to clarify a few points if I may in relation to my learned colleague and friend's submissions. With respect, and I guess this is where the parties diverge, I think that my friend's submission by trying to look and see how the prisoners were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. selected and, in focusing on the fact that he alleges that Mr. Martinovic department have any say into which prisoners were selected, misses the point. The fact that the focus of that part of his submissions is on whether or not the Prosecution can prove at that particular time at that particular place that they were taken on a discriminatory basis somewhat narrows the lens in a manner which the Prosecution submits is inconsistent with all of the evidence. As I indicated earlier, there were only Muslims taken. Muslims were not treated the same in the detention centre of the trial judgement at paragraph 431 actually indicates that Bosnian Croat detainees were permitted to go over to the side where the Muslim detainees were and to beat them. There were only Muslims taken from the Heliodrom. And when they arrive, I indicated five instances that I picked of those doing detention work where they were called derogatory names by Mr. Martinovic himself. It's inconceivable that this was random, that he actually likes call everyone by these derogatory names and they could in fact be Croats and he's just using that terminology for people who worked for him. At footnote 1685 which I referred to in my submission, Mr. Kerns pointed out that the Trial Chamber was satisfied that Mr. Martinovic would use enemy soldiers instead of his own soldiers. I accept that's what the trier found and that's the basis upon which they had the reasonable doubt. As you know, in relation to the wooden rifle incidents he referred to that two of the three were actually Muslim HV. So soldiers so they weren't enemy soldiers. One of them, Witness PP, had been in hospital for an operation and was taken out of the hospital, and Witness I, who was the witness to it, was also a Muslim HVO soldier so it's hard to imagine how the Court came to the conclusion that they were enemy soldiers. What they were, were Muslims who they were against, not ABiH soldiers. And in relation 20 the civilians I mentioned earlier on, a number of the civilians listed in the unlawful labour section of the judgement from 268 to 270, I think I was able to find three of them were civilians, including witness KK who was a 16 year old boy. In relation to the fact that there was evidence that Mr. Martinovic may have helped some Muslims I just ask you to refer not only to the passage Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen -- I mean, Judge Schomburg referred to but also at paragraph 678 of the judgement. The didn't accept that as a basis for undermining the discriminatory intent. If I could just speak about Mr. Par's factual submissions because, with respect, that's all they were, he claims by showing you the picture that nobody came to work at the front line, nobody could have worked there, and nobody could have dug trenches at the front line and basically indicated that there was no work done there. All I'd ask you to do is look at the footnotes I referred to in my submission. Footnote 722, 723, 725, and 727. All of them indicate that Witness J's work consisted of filling sandbags and digging trenches to fill the bags and he had to cross the line. Witness PP had to take bunkers apart destroy trenches sometimes in the line of fire, and Witness Allan Knudsen testified that prisoners were working on the front line all the time. With respect the factual representations are not consistent with the judgement. And simply, lastly Mr. Kerns points to the Prosecution's submissions as requiring a reversal of the onus. The Prosecution is more than willing to accept the Krnojelac appeals Chamber judgement where it indicates that based on the context and the surrounding circumstances that may, and in this case, it's our submission, it does, leave no reasonable doubt. That's all I wanted to address from the Prosecution side for the first ground of appeal. I understand that Mr. Kremer has no submissions in relation to the second issue, deportation. Mr. Tracol indicated he would have a few minutes just on the cumulative convictions in relation to Mr. Naletilic's comments before lunch. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tracol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, briefly, may I reply. As far as the response of the Prosecution is concerned concerning fourth ground of appeal where the Defence responded to a while ago. I would just like to respond on two points. The first relates to a -- crime elements, i.e. persecution and torture. The second point has to do with the standard applied for cumulative convictions in the case of persecution and other crimes against humanity. As far as the first point is concerned, namely crime elements, first of all, we are talking about persecution. The Appeals Chamber defined the crime of persecution in the Krnojelac judgement in paragraph 185 and applied the applicable test for cumulative conviction, applied it to persecution and other crimes against humanity in Kordic and Cerkez, in paragraph 1044 and following. As far as the torture elements are concerned, there is a jurisprudence provided by the Appeals Chamber in this particular instance. Please refer to the Kunarac judgement paragraph 142 and 144. The Defence submitted towards the end of the morning that each act of torture must have a discriminatory intent and in practice each act of torture involves a discriminatory process. This is not the position held by the Defence because, according to the definition which was provided by the Appeals Chamber in the Kunarac judgement, in the paragraphs 142 and 142 [as interpreted], the mens rea element in torture is requires a specific intent. In other words, with a view to obtaining a confession, so to punish and force the victims or to provide discriminatory intent, for whatever reason it may be, discrimination therefore is an alternative element and part of torture, but is not a part and parcel of the torture element so as far as cumulative conviction is concerned the proof of discrimination is not required as regards mens rea -- the involvement of mens rea in torture, if the Defence disagrees with the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber, i.e. the Krnojelac and Kunarac judgement a definition of these crimes has been provided by the Appeals Chamber. The Defence therefore is free to prove to the Chamber that for compelling reasons i.e., in the interests of justice for the Chamber to move away from this decision. Paragraph 108 of Kowalowski [phoen] and the Defence this morning didn't even make an attempt to prove any of these compelling reasons. As far as the second point is concerned, this has to do with the cumulative conviction for persecution and other crimes against humanity, and the standard that is applied in those cases. The Defence referred in a number of cases towards the end of the morning to the Krstic judgement. The Defence seemed to forget that the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement considered that compelling reasons commanded them to move away from the Krstic judgement because this -- in this case, the standard was not applied correctly. There was a murder and persecution, and that applicable law, when referring to cumulative conviction for persecution and other crimes against humanity and therefore the Kordic and Cerkez judgement was referred to this morning. I have now provided my response and I'm prepared to answer any of your questions, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe there are no questions. So may I take it that the Prosecution has concluded its reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So then, if the parties have concluded submissions, we can move on to the personal addresses of the accused, if they wish to avail themselves of this possibility. And I will ask Mr. Naletilic if he wants to address now the Bench. According to what I said this morning, Mr. Naletilic, you will have 20 minutes for your address. So please bear that in mind. You have the floor. THE APPELLANT NALETILIC: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused. THE APPELLANT NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for the five minutes that you gave me. I would like briefly to start with the founding of the Convicts' Battalion. It was established in 1991. The Court established specifically that I was its commander, its first commander, and I was its commander until the 15th of August 1992. Then Mario Hrkac, Cikota, and there is a decree on that, was appointed upon my initiative as not a formal but a formal and practical head. I would just like to say something about this legend ascribed to me. I think that Sir Martin Garrod said that Tuta is legendary. I laughed then because I always believed that only a dead man could turn into a legend and that's what Mario Hrkac, Cikota, was for me now today. He was a legend. I think that I created this fame. I think that I ascribed most of the qualities to him. I imbued him with all the qualities that he has. He was a child when he came to me. He was 18 years old. He grew into a leader whom I sincerely admired. I always thought of him the best had he remained alive. Had he become a footballer he would have been the best. Had he been an athlete he would have been a world champion. He was a natural mixture of intellect and force. I watched the actions that he carried out. My last action was at Debelo Brdo and also he could see that I was finished, I could not go on any longer. I weighed 56 kilograms. Let me just point out the difference for you how good the prisons are. When I went into prison, I had 56 kilograms. Today I weigh 80 kilograms. I'm not saying this in order to evade responsibility. I am still faithful to my beliefs. I will always remain responsible. Mario was killed on the 20th of April 1993. The Prosecution -- I heard a lot about Mario being this and that, but Tuta was there all the time. There is no doubt that I would always stand by him as much as I could. But nobody noticed here actually what it means to be a commander. A commander is only as good as the soldiers who sense him. The moment when he no longer can follow his soldiers to wherever they go to, he's finished. He cannot be a commander any longer. He can remain so by name but a commander is always the person who is somewhere first. At Debelo Brdo, I did that action, I also did the Velez and the Pod Velez actions as well. Debelo Brdo was my last action. That was when he understood that I felt at the weakest point. I could feel him feel sorry for me. He said, Old man it's not going any more. And I said, No it's not. Of course I always stood by him. I helped him as much as I could. And now when we are talking about the Doljani and Sovici actions, that action is not one that was headed by Tuta. This was a complex action and had it been carried out in 1992 I would not have been able to carry it out. We were specialised and we remained that. We specialised for the most difficult assignments but once for a maximum of 60 people. My unit or capacity was not greater than that. I was very good but Cikota was the best. At the time Cikota was given the Pasije Stene, that was an elevation over Sovici and Doljani. I don't know the elevation. It could be up to 1.000 metres. When that fell, everything else would fall because in each strategy there is a point in time when -- where that -- it's used as a stronghold, and when this stronghold is captured then everything falls after that. Even a child could then continue on after the stronghold falls. Mario was given that assignment. He carried it out perfectly. He went around the hill above Sovici and Doljani. I don't know that road. I wasn't there. But he took the road. He reached elevation 905 and that was when he -- when it fell. And he deserved it. I was with some children, some 30 kilometres away. You have to know one thing. I think Udo had five years and Mate was five -- five years old. They didn't speak Croatian. No matter how long I spent in jail, I consider myself to be a good father. Perhaps I was not a good husband but I was certainly a good father. I would never have left my children for three and four days in order to go out on an action. That was impossible, had it even been in 1992. When the late Boka was killed I knew that I had to go and I went there. There is no doubt that as soon as I went to Doljani there was a small creek there, I went across and I saw them kneeling, five, six, ten prisoners. I don't know how many of them were there. Immediately I said, stand up, get up. I said, Who was the commander? Actually there were no commanders any more. There were soldiers. Not our soldiers because Alija was in Sipica Livade [phoen]. So when they were coming down, Marica Kuce is ten kilometres away, and Cikota was at elevation 905 which is also ten kilometres away. So there were no soldiers there. Our soldiers did not shoot. I didn't see anybody being beaten. There were stories here about some grape-picking and so on. I said get up. You must not beat them. No one was beaten as long as I was there. Some people said there was also one young boy a soldier came to me, I don't know why he came to me and said, well, we have an underage person. Would you ask the commander to let him go? I said, son, take that child home. And if anybody has anything against that, let them come to me. But then the first testimony that was seen here and he obviously remembers me but he didn't mention any beating or being hit or anything like that. But in 1996, the statements changed. I'm not going to talk about that. I read all the statements since 1993. Nobody mentioned me. They mentioned Tutici and I will speak about that. I did write about that. When I took Boka, I went to Risovac, up there where my children were, and I took them and then the next day something else happened. Cikota was killed. I don't need to say more. I mean, I can sincerely say that I felt that he was just like my own child. I loved him. So it was a blow to me, too. Witnesses, who do I know were saying Tuta was in Sovici and Doljani. I don't know which dates. But in any case, they got their reasons. I think that Judge Pocar saw documents, he rejected them but he saw them where it is stated that 26 people were suspected as being indicted by The Hague but Tuta's name was not among those names. But the problem actually then was created for the commander, even was ideal. But he had a problem. He was suffering from diabetes, so it wasn't sure that he could carry out that task. But he got it. He got this task, and as far as the operative aspect is concerned, he did his best. Would I have helped? Yes. Was I able to go into actions? No, no, you have to know that I am suffering from emphysema. My lungs were not functioning properly, my breathing wasn't so good. My heart, of course, would be placed under stress in that situation. So I was also suffering from a heart ailment. But there was no way out. I was charged with persecutions and I would like you to carefully look me in the eye. Here I would never order or carry out anybody else's orders, neither did I ever issue any order to that effect, personally. I'm not only speaking ethically. I remember when I was an immigrant there was a famous professor who used to say there was no death penalty in ancient Greece. That was not the worst punishment. The worst punishment was to be expelled from one's homeland, to be banished. As far as I'm concerned, this is something that was absolutely out of the question. As far as Sovici and Doljani is concerned, I think that this was some time later, in May, in early May. And now I would like the name to be entered correctly into the transcript. Perhaps you will be needing it, perhaps the Prosecution will in any case, because this is very important. Miro Gradovac, called Gida [phoen], came. He came to me, not to Andabak, and our soldier from Posusje and he said, Old man are you going to allow this? They are taking women, children, the elderly and they are taking them to the school. I don't know whether it was the secondary school, but in any case he described it. I said, Son, we will not allow that to happen. Where are the children? The women? And he said, Old man, they are up there. And I told Ivan, Give me some soldiers. I'm going to go there. We went there. I'm going to describe the building. It had a glass front. I don't know whether it was a sports hall because of the glass but it had to be some kind of sports venue. Everything was strewn around. There was nobody there. I just told Ivan we have been betrayed by our own people. Somebody must have let them know. You can check that. They went to the HQ in Posusje and we were told they were transferred to Vakuf. I swear that I would have had to be a paramilitary then to carry out an operation and I would have been. I mean we had come with rifles, we were not going to kindergarten. Had I done it I would have carried out the action perfectly. Anyway, that was finished. Then the Mostar action came later. Ivan was given the assignment in the direction of the old bridge. If you look at the television footage, I'm going to tell you about a case where I am 100 per cent guilty. You can interpret it psychologically however you want, but this is how it happened. Juka Prazina called me, had to have been in the afternoon. I had a Kenwood Motorola at the time, and it's important to look at the tape and you will see that I was in civilian clothing. Stari, he said, I have a surprise for you. I said, Tell me. He said, Come in front of the ministry. I have captured I don't know how many people. And then they came. The witness who came to testify here, I don't want to tell him his name because we are having the same kind of problem in Croatia at the moment, I cannot remember. Z was in the Heliodrom but I will also talk about him. It's very important. Judge Pocar said that he was interested in Witness Z. Anyway, this is what happened. Brana Kvesic, I suddenly heard him say, My God, what the hell are you doing here? And I looked, and it was that witness there. And then I saw that he was being aggressive. He came up to me. I was very good. He was broader and stronger than me and you can see that on the footage. I caught him from the back and we were tussling a bit, and then here he said that I struck him six times with the Motorola and that he was asked, Where are the scars, and, well, anyway, this is not what happened. But Alica Povric, a man who was at my wedding with me. Actually it was the marriage of Bozo Sain, a Muslim. I was the best man. We spent the whole evening together. There were Juka's people there. Our people from the Convicts' Battalion. There were many soldiers. I remember him well. He behaved as if he was sitting in the drawing room. He was different from the others. He said to me, Do you know this guy? I turned around and I said, You're one of us. I meant one of us from the Convicts' Battalion. He said, No, I'm not, Stari. And then when he said "Stari," I said, So then you must have fired at us? And he said, Yes, I did, Stari. So like this, you're not our soldier. Only our soldiers called me by that term, Stari. And friends. So -- and I grabbed my Motorola. He pulled back as a reflection. The Motorola did not hit him but it fell and it broke apart. But it was a very ugly scene. Juka Prazina, well it was a compliment to me, said, What happened to you, Stari? I said, What do you mean what happened? He betrayed us. And then he said to me, Tuta, I did not betray you. I'm Arif Pasalic's driver. I know you. How could you be his driver? He said, Yes, we were at the wedding. Then it all came back to me. This is what happened, Juka Prazina -- how much time do I have left, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Another four minutes. THE APPELLANT NALETILIC: [Interpretation] Four? I said, Well, I asked you not to hand him over. He was taken to Zagreb, to the embassy. That was his desire and he is still working there to this very day. He did not come here to testify. So he's that incident with the Motorola. I will be very brief. Neither I nor Cikota, late Cikota, nor Andabak commanded any ATG group. No other battalion other than the Convicts' Battalion. Neither -- there was a sister group, that was the Baja Kraljevic ATG. That was the group that went with us. Predrag was the commander and Cikota, and later it was Ivan and Ilija. Only they. Yesterday, Mr. -- somebody from the Prosecution said something about the HV. I never commanded the HV, and thank God that I did not because personally I did not have a very good opinion of them. I always believed that they were just there in order to acquire ranks, not really to wage war. And I would like to finish this. Your Honours, I have been charged with persecution. I am not guilty of that. I did save some people and the Trial Chamber saw that well. I'm not asking mercy for anything. I've already received mercy from God. I'm healthy. My children are healthy and all of that is fine. Regarding the prison, maybe you can give me another two minutes more. Mr. Martinovic said that I could take 8 minutes from him. Perhaps if you allow me two more minutes for me to say something which is very important about the prisons. Heliodrom, I was never there in 1993. Ljubuski, Siroki Brijeg, I never went to any of those prisons personally. The first and last time that I went to a prison was in 1994 in May. That is Witness Z whom I wanted to substitute for Ivankovic, exchange him for Ivankovic. The exchange didn't take place because he didn't want to because he knew that he was going to be released soon anyway. Aleksovski was the camp commander and he was there in 1993. This can be checked. Witness Z, when I told him, Okay, if you don't want to, we are finished, you can go. He stayed. And at that point in time, my driver, who was standing right behind him, grabbed him by the collar and lifted him up. I jumped up immediately. I swore I don't want to do that here. I told him, Get out. I apologised to him. I apologised to Aleksovski and when I went out he said to me, Stari you shouldn't have humiliated me like that. And I swore and I said, This is the last time that you're coming with me. That's the truth and as far as what he said about me knowing that he stole some money from the fourth, I didn't know. And had I known I would have said, You're a revolutionary, you took the opponent's money. I didn't want to charge him with that, absolutely not. So Siroki Brijeg, I don't have time but maybe it would be important to you. Had I known as the same way that I knew about Dobra Kurdice [phoen], had I known that anybody was committing beatings in Siroki Brijeg I would have punished them. But I see that I am at the end of my time. In 1994, I went to the Lisak cemetery to pay my respect to the witness -- to the victims, the only Croat. I also wish to express my deepest sympathy to the families of all those killed, Serbs, Muslims, as well as foreigners. There were many of them who gave their lives in Herzegovina. I would also like to express my sympathy for those who suffered the torture of expulsion. I have finished. I think, Your Honours. I think I don't have any more time. I don't want to go over the time. I would like to also thank my lawyers, Mr. Matthew Hennessy and Mr. Christopher Meek who really devoted themselves completely to have the best arguments in these appeals and I would also like to thank you the lawyers of Vinko Martinovic, Stela. I would also like to express my respect for the Prosecution. I must admit that I have learnt a lot here because I used to believe that everything strives for the truth. But I am no longer sure of that. And to you, Your Honours, I would like to thank you too for allowing me to speak. If you would give me another minute just to say something about the prison in Croatia, where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic I already gave you five additional minutes. So please. THE APPELLANT NALETILIC: [Interpretation]. I apologise. I apologise. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I now turn to Mr. Martinovic, if he wants to address the Court, he has 15 minutes. THE APPELLANT MARTINOVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you for allowing me to address you, Your Honours. I realise that war is an evil in which it is mostly the ordinary and the little people who suffer. I sympathise with them and I respect and regret anything that happened to any victim and the only thing that we as little people can do is to help each other amidst this evil. It is said that this is the Court of truth and justice, and this is why I have to say that there are many reasons due to which I do not accept this conviction. I did not take part in the murder of the prisoners Nenad Harmandzic. I did not abuse the prisoners, nor did I place them in the human shield. I was convicted for taking part in the murder based on a false testimony of a mentally ill witness. The secret services of Croatia and Bosnia joined forces in order to bring me here and conceal the actual people who issued orders and those who executed them. It was the easiest thing to bring me here because I was not familiar with the military and political plans. It was easiest to sacrifice an ordinary soldier on whose behalf nobody would intercede. This is why I would like this court to review evidence pertaining to this charge of the indictment. Your Honours, I never allowed anybody from the work group to be abused in my unit or in my vicinity. I allowed my attorneys to explain my role in the war in Mostar because I do not understand this trial, these proceedings, at all. I was an ordinary soldier in the war which took place in front of my house. I did not want this war. It was here before this Court that I heard for the first time that I took part in an international conflict. My neighbours, Muslims, Jews, Serbs, and Croats who testified in these proceedings, showed to you, Your Honours, that I do not hate anybody because of their religion or of their ethnicity. Nor did I ever harbour any hatred within me. It is true that I'm not an educated man but even without a rule book I know that it is impermissible to abuse or mistreat a prisoner. I never allowed that kind of actions to take place. However, it is the Prosecution who claims that a person was killed while under my protection and I would like to assure you from the bottom of my heart that that did not take place in my unit. And this is something that is illustrated by the documentation of the Prosecution. Their documentation shows who is responsible for what happened to that man. I should not have been convicted for that. Everybody knew, it was visible to everybody that he escaped from the military police and then the military police reported that. Now I am faced with a 18-year prison sentence and I was sentenced for something that never even occurred to me, let alone concealed something like that. I heard in Mostar when they asked this mentally ill witness, Why did you lie in The Hague?, he responded, I am crazy but I am not that crazy so as to refuse the house that was given to me for two hours of lying. There is what this witness who testified about the murder said. More difficult than the sentence is the false testimony and I felt it on my own skin. I was convicted to 18 years of prison because I did not enter into plea bargain with the Prosecution. And how could I explain that there was nothing to me to bargain about because I did not abuse anybody, I did not mistreat anybody, let alone kill anybody. If I could somehow explain to you, Your Honours, my role at the demarcation line, what I did and under what circumstances, you would acquit me. However, I don't know how to explain that. It would have been easier for me if you were to put questions to me. It took seven years for a new indictment to be issued for acts committed in Mostar, and the indictment was issued only after I was convicted. They did everything in order to attribute everything bad that happened in the war in Mostar to Stela. I was told this personally by the people indicted in the new indictment as well as by the people who are with me at the Detention Unit. We have a saying in Mostar, in Zagreb, that even birds in the trees know what secret services did to Martinovic and Naletilic. However, it is really bad that those who should know - and that is you, Your Honours - do not know about what was done in the proceedings against us. It is a shame, Your Honours, that the Appeals Chamber refused to hear new witnesses. Justice will not be served by that. Had those people come to testify before this Court, then everything would have become clear to you. You would know why is it that 14 witnesses were prepared to testify against me and what was given to them in exchange for the testimony against me. And I think that the gentleman from the Prosecution know very well about this. Not only did this affect the judgement, but had it not been for this, this judgement would not have been rendered. We were unable to bring these witnesses here to testify before because at that time, the secret services, both the Croatian one and the Muslim one were active. Now those services are disbanded and all the dirty laundry has emerged. It hurts me that I was lumped together with the most serious criminals and those who insincerely repented. Those who insincerely repented, once they returned to the Detention Unit upon receiving a very short sentence, they boast about their crimes. And this is not good for the victims and their families. I had to say this. It is very hard for me to keep quiet about this. Sometimes I lose hope that I will be able to go back to life and participate in the upbringing of my son but if God desires it, then I am prepared to persevere and to carry on. Today I'm aware of the mistakes that I've made in my life. However, I do not wish to be held responsible for acts that I did not commit. I know that I am not important for this Court or for any state, any country. However, for my son and for my wife, despite of everything, I am the most important. And I need to play a positive role in their life. If you, Your Honours, believe that I did not do enough to help the people in Mostar, then, yes, I'm guilty. But I assure you that during wartime, under the war circumstances, I did everything within my power, that of an ordinary man, an ordinary soldier. I did the best I could in order to help people whom I was able to help, regardless of their religion or ethnicity. I believe in God and I expect a just judgement. Thank you for allowing me to express my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Martinovic. You can sit down. This concludes the appeal. I would like to -- before adjourning, I would like to, on behalf of the Bench, to thank the parties for their submissions, and for answering the questions posed by the Bench. I would like also to express our thanks to all the staff who had a role in this meeting, and of course to the interpreters that made our hearing more efficient. The hearing stands now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.16 p.m.
